questions.e: The threshold stimulus is the minimum stimulus that produces a muscle twitch. Sub-threshold stimuli fail to elicit any contractile response.

questions.q: The latent period of a muscle twitch lasts about:
questions.e: The latent period lasts approximately 2 milliseconds — the time between stimulation and the onset of force generation, corresponding to the time required for Ca2+ release from the SR.

questions.q: During the relaxation phase of a muscle twitch, which process occurs?
o: ATP hydrolysis energizes the myosin head
Ca2+ is actively transported back into the SR
questions.e: During relaxation, Ca2+ is actively transported back into the SR by the Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) pump, lowering sarcoplasmic Ca2+ and allowing tropomyosin to re-block actin sites.

questions.q: Type I muscle fibers are best characterized as:
o: Slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant, rich in myoglobin
questions.e: Type I (Slow Oxidative) fibers are loaded with mitochondria, rich in myoglobin (red), highly fatigue-resistant, have extensive blood supply, and are innervated by slow-conducting small neurons.

questions.q: Which type of muscle fiber is DOMINANT in muscles responsible for maintaining posture?
questions.e: Type I (Slow Oxidative) fibers dominate postural muscles because they are highly fatigue-resistant, enabling sustained low-level activity needed to maintain posture continuously.

questions.q: Type IIb (Fast Glycolytic) fibers have all of the following characteristics EXCEPT:
o: High in myoglobin giving a reddish color
questions.e: Type IIb fibers are LOW in myoglobin, giving them a WHITISH color. They have few mitochondria, depend on glycolysis, are rich in glycogen, and fatigue easily.

questions.q: True or False: Type IIa fibers are activated by large-diameter, fast-conducting motor neurons.
questions.e: FALSE. Type IIa fibers are activated by medium-sized neurons. It is Type IIb (Fast Glycolytic) fibers that are activated by LARGE-diameter, fast-conducting motor neurons.

questions.q: Type IIa muscle fibers are best suited for which type of activity?
questions.e: Type IIa (Fast Oxidative) fibers use both cellular respiration and glycolysis, making them moderately fatigue-resistant and well-suited for middle-distance endurance activities.

questions.q: Wave summation occurs when a muscle is stimulated:
o: Before the relaxation phase of a previous twitch is complete
By two different motor neurons simultaneously
questions.e: Wave summation occurs when a second stimulus arrives BEFORE the muscle fully relaxes from the previous twitch, resulting in greater force than a single twitch.

questions.q: True or False: Summation is possible because contraction and relaxation phases are much shorter than the refractory period.
questions.e: FALSE. Summation is possible because contraction and relaxation phases are MUCH LONGER than the refractory period, allowing re-stimulation before full relaxation.

questions.q: The reason rapid stimulation produces greater force (wave summation) is primarily because:
o: The sarcolemma becomes more permeable to Na+
There is insufficient time to remove all Ca2+ from the sarcoplasm
ATP regenerates faster during rapid stimulation
questions.e: With rapid stimulation, insufficient time exists to pump all Ca2+ back into the SR. Elevated sarcoplasmic Ca2+ means more active cross-bridge formation and greater contractile force.

questions.q: A smooth, sustained contraction with NO relaxation between stimuli is called:
questions.e: Complete (fused) tetanus occurs when stimulation is so rapid that no relaxation occurs between twitches, producing a smooth sustained contraction about 4 times greater than a single twitch.

questions.q: The tension developed during complete tetanus compared to a single twitch is approximately:
questions.e: Complete tetanus produces tension approximately 4 times that of a single twitch due to sustained elevated sarcoplasmic Ca2+ and maximum cross-bridge formation throughout.

questions.q: True or False: Incomplete (unfused) tetanus shows partial relaxation between successive stimuli.
questions.e: TRUE. Incomplete tetanus shows PARTIAL relaxation between twitches; complete tetanus shows NO relaxation. Both produce greater force than individual twitches.

questions.q: The Treppe (staircase) phenomenon refers to:
o: Gradual decrease in force with repeated stimulation
Wave summation at a threshold stimulus only
A sudden large increase in force at tetanizing frequency
Gradual increase in contractile force with repeated stimuli at slightly below tetanizing frequency
questions.e: Treppe is the gradual, stepwise increase in contractile force with repeated stimuli at a frequency slightly below the tetanizing frequency, believed due to increased Ca2+ availability.

questions.q: The Treppe phenomenon is believed to be due to:
o: Increased availability of Ca2+ for troponin binding
questions.e: Treppe is believed to result from increased Ca2+ availability for troponin binding, possibly due to incomplete Ca2+ reuptake between stimuli at the given frequency.

questions.q: The PASSIVE tension curve in the length-tension relationship arises from:
questions.e: Passive tension in an unstimulated stretched muscle is ascribed to the elasticity of titin, which acts as molecular springs between the Z-disc and M-line.

questions.q: Maximal active tension in a muscle fiber develops at the length that allows:
o: Maximum overlap of thick filaments only
Maximum overlap between thin and thick filaments without filament interference
Minimum overlap between thick and thin filaments
Complete separation of thick and thin filaments
questions.e: Maximal tension develops at the optimal (resting) length where maximum productive overlap between thin and thick filaments occurs WITHOUT thin filaments from opposite sides interfering.

questions.q: At very SHORT sarcomere lengths, active tension is LOW because:
o: Calcium cannot bind to troponin at short lengths
Thin filaments from both sides of the M-line interfere with each other
Myosin heads cannot physically reach actin
questions.e: At very short sarcomere lengths, thin filaments from opposite sides overlap and interfere with each other at the M-line, reducing cross-bridge formation and active tension.

questions.q: True or False: The length-tension relationship supports the sliding filament theory by showing that tension depends on the degree of overlap between actin and myosin filaments.
questions.e: TRUE. The length-tension relationship validates the sliding filament theory: maximal tension at optimal overlap confirms that cross-linkages between actin and myosin generate contractile tension.

questions.q: The muscle length at which maximal active tension is produced is known as the:
questions.e: The optimal (resting) length is the sarcomere length at which maximal active tension is generated due to maximum productive overlap between thick and thin filaments.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is best classified as:
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is a type of involuntary striated muscle found only in the heart — it shares the striated (banded) appearance of skeletal muscle but contracts without conscious control.

questions.q: What is the primary functional role of cardiac muscle?
o: To pump blood through the circulatory system
To store glycogen for the body
questions.e: Cardiac muscle's defining job is mechanical — it pumps blood through the circulatory system with every contraction.

questions.q: How are cardiac muscle cells typically described morphologically?
o: Spindle-shaped single-nucleus cells only, no branching
questions.e: Cardiac muscle cells are branched and interlace with one another, unlike the long parallel fibres of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Compared with skeletal muscle, the cross-striations in cardiac muscle are:
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is striated, but its cross-striations are less distinct than those seen in skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle activity is innervated and modulated by which system?
questions.e: Although cardiac muscle is myogenic (self-exciting), it is innervated by the autonomic nervous system, which modulates rate and force.

questions.q: In terms of nucleation, cardiac muscle cells are typically:
questions.e: Unlike multinucleate skeletal muscle fibres, cardiac myocytes are predominantly mononucleate.

questions.q: Cardiac myocytes contain numerous, large, well-developed mitochondria mainly because:
o: They store calcium instead of the SR
They rely on continuous, high aerobic energy demand
Mitochondria replace the need for sarcomeres
questions.e: The heart beats continuously and relies heavily on oxidative metabolism, which is reflected in the high density of large mitochondria.

questions.q: Compared with skeletal muscle fibres, cardiac myocytes are:
questions.e: Cardiac myocytes are narrower and much shorter than skeletal muscle cells.

questions.q: Intercalated discs, which join cardiac cells end to end, contain which structures that permit electrical continuity?
questions.e: Gap junctions within intercalated discs provide low-resistance pathways that let the action potential pass rapidly from cell to cell.

questions.q: What structure provides mechanical (rather than electrical) linkage between cardiac cells at the intercalated disc?
questions.e: Desmosomes mechanically link adjacent cardiac cells, helping the tissue withstand the mechanical stress of repeated contraction.

questions.q: Because electrical current spreads freely between cardiac cells via gap junctions, cardiac muscle functions as a:
questions.e: The electrical continuity provided by gap junctions allows cardiac muscle to behave functionally as a single unit, or syncytium.

questions.q: The contractile filaments of cardiac muscle (actin and myosin) are organised into:
o: Sarcomeres, just as in skeletal muscle
Fused continuous filaments with no units
Random bundles with no repeating unit
questions.e: Cardiac muscle shares its fundamental contractile unit, the sarcomere, with skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle is false?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic/myogenic — it generates its own action potentials at the SA node and does not require neural stimulation to contract (though the ANS modulates rate and force).

questions.q: How many T-tubules are associated with each sarcomere in cardiac muscle, and where are they located?
o: One, located close to the Z-line
questions.e: Cardiac muscle has only one T-tubule per sarcomere, positioned near the Z-line — unlike skeletal muscle's two T-tubules per sarcomere at the A–I junctions.

questions.q: In cardiac muscle, a T-tubule associates with a single terminal cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum to form a structure called a:
questions.e: This single T-tubule/single-cisterna pairing is called a diad, in contrast with the triads (one T-tubule, two cisternae) of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: How developed is the sarcoplasmic reticulum of cardiac muscle relative to skeletal muscle?
questions.e: The cardiac SR is much less developed (more sparse) than that of skeletal myofibres, which has direct consequences for calcium handling during contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle is true?
o: Ca2+ plays an important role in repolarization of the membrane
Ca2+ play no role in the process of contraction
Ca2+ are not released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
About half the Ca2+ required for contraction comes from outside the cell
Ca2+ do not bind to troponin
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. In cardiac muscle (unlike skeletal muscle), roughly half the activator Ca2+ enters from the extracellular space via L-type Ca2+ channels, triggering further Ca2+ release from the SR (calcium-induced calcium release).

questions.q: The prepotential of the pacemaker action potential is by
o: an inward flow of Ca2+ through T-type Ca2+ channels
a slow inward flow of Na+
an inward flow of K+ through T-type K+ channels
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The pacemaker (prepotential) slope is generated by a slow inward 'funny' Na+ current, followed later by a T-type Ca2+ current as threshold approaches — options a and b.

questions.q: Phase 0 of the non-pacemaker cardiac action potential is caused primarily by:
o: Closure of all K⁺ channels permanently
questions.e: Phase 0, the rapid depolarization phase, results from opening of fast Na⁺ channels, sharply increasing g_Na and driving a rapid Na⁺ influx (I_Na).

questions.q: During phase 0 of the non-pacemaker AP, what happens to outward K⁺ conductance?
o: It falls, as K⁺ channels close
questions.e: As fast Na⁺ channels open, g_K+ falls and outward K⁺ currents decline, helping move the membrane potential toward E_Na.

questions.q: Phase 1 (initial repolarization) of the non-pacemaker AP occurs mainly due to:
o: A second wave of Ca²⁺ influx
Inactivation of fast Na⁺ channels, plus a transient outward K⁺ current and Cl⁻ efflux
questions.e: Phase 1 begins when the fast Na⁺ channels inactivate; a brief outward K⁺ current together with Cl⁻ efflux produces the characteristic early notch.

questions.q: Which two currents are specifically implicated in Phase 1's small repolarization notch?
o: Transient outward K⁺ current and Cl⁻ efflux
Funny current and T-type Ca²⁺ current
questions.e: Phase 1's notch is produced by a transient net outward K⁺ current together with Cl⁻ efflux, following Na⁺ channel inactivation.

questions.q: The plateau (phase 2) of the cardiac action potential is sustained by a balance between:
o: Inward Ca²⁺ current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels and outward K⁺ current through slow delayed rectifier channels
questions.e: The plateau reflects a near-balance between inward Ca²⁺ (I_Ca, via L-type Ca²⁺ channels) and outward K⁺ current (I_Ks, the slow delayed rectifier).

questions.q: Which calcium channel type is responsible for the inward current sustaining the plateau phase?
questions.e: L-type Ca²⁺ channels carry the inward I_Ca current that helps sustain the plateau phase (phase 2).

questions.q: Phase 3 (final repolarization) of the non-pacemaker AP involves:
o: Sustained opening of L-type Ca²⁺ channels
Complete cessation of all ion flow
Closure of L-type Ca²⁺ channels alongside opening of I_Kr and I_K1, producing net outward current
questions.e: In phase 3, L-type Ca²⁺ channels close, I_Ks remains open, and I_Kr plus I_K1 open — producing a net outward, positive current that repolarizes the cell.

questions.q: Which potassium current continues to conduct throughout phase 4, contributing to the resting membrane potential?
questions.e: I_K1, the inwardly rectifying K⁺ current, remains conducting throughout phase 4 and helps set the resting membrane potential.

questions.q: Approximately what value does the membrane potential return to at the start of phase 4 in the non-pacemaker AP?
questions.e: Delayed rectifier K⁺ channels close once the membrane potential is restored to about −80 to −85 mV, marking the start of phase 4.

questions.q: The Na⁺–K⁺ pump restores ionic gradients after each action potential by exchanging Na⁺ for K⁺ in what ratio?
questions.e: The Na⁺–K⁺ pump exchanges Na⁺ for K⁺ in a 3:2 ratio, extruding 3 Na⁺ ions for every 2 K⁺ ions brought in.

questions.q: Pacemaker tissues are defined by their ability to:
o: Contract only in response to external stimuli
Exhibit automaticity — generating regular, spontaneous action potentials
questions.e: Pacemaker cells exhibit automaticity: they spontaneously generate regular action potentials without needing external stimulation, unlike working myocardium.

questions.q: Which of the following lists the components of the heart's conduction system?
o: Only the SA node and AV node
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibres, internodal pathways
Bundle of His and coronary sinus only
questions.e: The conduction system comprises the SA node, atrial internodal pathways, the AV node, the Bundle of His, and Purkinje fibres.

questions.q: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous depolarization and normally sets the heart rate.

questions.q: How does the resting potential of pacemaker cells differ from that of non-pacemaker cardiac cells?
o: Pacemaker cells lack any membrane potential
Pacemaker cells have a more negative, stable resting potential
Pacemaker cells have an identical resting potential to non-pacemaker cells
Pacemaker cells have no true resting potential — they continuously depolarize
questions.e: Pacemaker cells have no true (stable) resting potential; instead they undergo continuous, spontaneous depolarization (automaticity).

questions.q: The channel responsible for the initiation of spontaneous depolarization in phase 4 of the SA node cell exhibits which of the following properties?
o: It is opened by membrane depolarization
It is opened by vagal nerve stimulation
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. This describes the funny current (Iꜰ) channel — unusual because it is activated by hyperpolarization/repolarization (not depolarization) at the end of the previous action potential, and it conducts a net inward, depolarizing current that is primarily carried by Na⁺. Vagal stimulation (ACh) actually slows it down, and norepinephrine enhances (not closes) it — both B, C and E describe the opposite of what actually happens.

questions.q: At approximately what membrane potential does a pacemaker cell reach threshold and trigger phase 0?
questions.e: The slow phase 4 depolarization continues until the threshold potential, roughly −40 to −50 mV, is reached.

questions.q: Phase 0 of the pacemaker action potential is due to an increase in conductance and inward current of which ion, through which channel type?
questions.e: Unlike non-pacemaker phase 0 (fast Na⁺-driven), pacemaker phase 0 depolarization is due to increased Ca²⁺ conductance and inward current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels.

questions.q: Repolarization (phase 3) of the pacemaker action potential occurs because:
o: Ca²⁺ conductance continues to rise indefinitely
Ca²⁺ channels rapidly inactivate, Na⁺ permeability decreases, and K⁺ conductance increases
questions.e: In pacemaker phase 3, Ca²⁺ channels inactivate rapidly, Na⁺ permeability falls, and K⁺ conductance rises, repolarizing the cell to about −60 mV before the cycle repeats.

questions.q: The resting potential range of a pacemaker cell (before spontaneous depolarization) is approximately:
questions.e: Pacemaker cells sit at roughly −60 mV to −70 mV, maintained by a continuous outward "leak" of K⁺, before slow depolarization begins.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is released during sympathetic activation of the SA node?
questions.e: Sympathetic activation releases norepinephrine (NE) onto the SA node.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effect of sympathetic activation on pacemaker rate?
o: Has no measurable effect on ion conductances
Decreases g_K+ and enhances the pacemaker current, increasing rate
Increases g_K+ and suppresses I_f, decreasing rate
questions.e: Sympathetic activation decreases g_K+, enhances I_f, and increases slow inward g_Ca2+ and g_Na+ — steepening phase 4 and increasing pacemaker rate.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter mediates parasympathetic (vagal) effects on the SA node?
questions.e: Parasympathetic (vagal) activation releases acetylcholine (ACh) onto the SA node.

questions.q: Parasympathetic (vagal) activation decreases pacemaker rate by:
o: Increasing g_K+ and suppressing the pacemaker current
questions.e: ACh increases g_K+, suppresses I_f, and decreases slow inward g_Ca2+ and g_Na+ currents, reducing the slope of phase 4 and slowing the rate at which threshold is reached.

questions.q: Regarding excitation–contraction coupling, which of the following is correct?
o: In the resting state, tropomyosin (not troponin itself) sterically blocks the myosin-binding site on actin
Relaxation occurs when Ca²⁺ is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA
The Ca²⁺ released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to tropomyosin
The muscle action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Excitation–contraction coupling begins with the action potential spreading along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules, which triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Note: Ca²⁺ actually binds troponin (not tropomyosin) which then shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding site — so the classic textbook statement in option B is a common trap. Option A is the accurate first step of the process.

questions.q: "Calcium-induced calcium release" in cardiac muscle refers to:
o: Calcium entering via L-type channels stimulating ryanodine-sensitive channels to release further Ca²⁺ from the SR
A process unique to skeletal, not cardiac, muscle
Calcium being pumped directly out of the cell
Calcium binding myosin instead of troponin
questions.e: Ca²⁺ entry through dihydropyridine-sensitive (L-type) channels triggers opening of ryanodine-sensitive channels in the SR, releasing more Ca²⁺ — calcium-induced calcium release.

questions.q: Why is Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum alone insufficient to fully activate contraction in cardiac muscle?
o: Because troponin C is absent in cardiac muscle
Because cardiac muscle has no T-tubules
Because the cardiac SR is relatively sparse compared with skeletal muscle
Because Ca²⁺ is toxic to cardiac cells
questions.e: Cardiac SR is relatively sparse (less developed), so SR-released Ca²⁺ must be augmented by Ca²⁺ entering through channels in the general sarcolemma, triggered by the AP.

questions.q: Calcium couples electrical excitation to contraction by binding to which protein?
questions.e: Ca²⁺ binds troponin C, which is attached to the actin filament, initiating the conformational changes that permit cross-bridge formation.

questions.q: During a twitch, Ca2+ binds to troponin during the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Ca2+ release and binding to troponin, along with cross-bridge cycling initiation, occurs during the latent period before tension development begins.

questions.q: Digitalis increases cardiac contractility primarily by:
o: Inhibiting the Na⁺ pump, leading to accumulation of cytosolic Ca²⁺
questions.e: Digitalis inhibits the Na⁺ pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase); the resulting rise in intracellular Na⁺ reduces the gradient driving Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange, causing cytosolic Ca²⁺ to accumulate and contractility to increase.

questions.q: Relaxation of cardiac muscle occurs mainly through which two calcium-removal mechanisms?
o: Ca²⁺ pumped back into the SR by a Ca²⁺-ATPase, and extruded via a Na⁺/Ca²⁺ antiporter plus sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase
Ca²⁺ diffuses passively with no active transport involved
Ca²⁺ is stored permanently in the nucleus
questions.e: Relaxation involves Ca²⁺ being pumped back into the SR by a Ca²⁺-ATPase (SERCA) and extruded to the extracellular fluid via a Na⁺/Ca²⁺ antiporter and a sarcolemmal Ca²⁺-ATPase.

questions.q: The tension developed in cardiac muscle
o: depends on the end diastolic volume
is proportional to the intracellular Ca2+ concentration
can be enhanced by the use of sodium pump inhibitors
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Tension depends on intracellular Ca2+ and on end-diastolic (preload) volume (Frank-Starling law). Sodium pump (Na+/K+ ATPase) inhibitors such as cardiac glycosides raise intracellular Na+, reduce Na+/Ca2+ exchange, and raise intracellular Ca2+ — enhancing contraction. So all three are correct.

questions.q: Which channel type initially admits the Ca²⁺ that triggers calcium-induced calcium release?
o: Dihydropyridine-sensitive channels in the sarcolemma/T-tubule membrane
questions.e: Dihydropyridine-sensitive (L-type) Ca²⁺ channels in the T-tubule membrane admit the initial trigger Ca²⁺, which then activates ryanodine receptors on the SR.

questions.q: The long plateau of the cardiac muscle action potential is due to
o: decrease in the amount of Ca2+ diffusing across the membrane
movement of fewer Na+ across the membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The plateau phase is maintained by sustained opening of L-type Ca2+ channels, which balances the outward K+ current and holds the membrane depolarized.

questions.q: Why can cardiac muscle not readily be tetanized?
o: Its refractory period extends beyond the end of the action potential
It contracts too slowly to summate at all
questions.e: Because the cardiac refractory period extends beyond the end of the AP, a new contraction cannot be triggered before the previous one ends, preventing tetanic summation.

questions.q: Why is the inability of cardiac muscle to tetanize functionally important?
o: Tetany of heart muscle would prevent effective pumping, since the heart must relax to refill
Tetanized cardiac muscle uses less oxygen
Tetany would allow more efficient pumping
questions.e: Effective pumping requires alternating contraction and relaxation so the chambers can refill; sustained tetanic contraction would abolish this cycle and stop the heart from pumping effectively.

questions.q: According to the length–tension relationship in cardiac muscle, an increase in preload (within limits) leads to:
o: An increase in active tension and the rate of its development
questions.e: Within limits, increasing preload (fibre length) increases both the active tension developed and the rate at which that tension develops.

questions.q: Unlike some other muscle types, cardiac muscle develops its maximum tension:
o: Only in the complete absence of Ca²⁺
Only at its shortest possible length
When stretched beyond its resting length
questions.e: Cardiac muscle's maximum developed tension occurs not at resting length, but when the muscle is stretched beyond resting length — up to physiological limits.

questions.q: Preload-driven increases in active tension are related to changes in:
o: The number of actin–myosin crosslinkages formed, and troponin C's sensitivity to calcium
questions.e: Stretch increases active tension by increasing the number of actin-myosin crosslinkages that can form and by increasing troponin C's sensitivity to calcium.

questions.q: In the heart
o: the SA node is located in the right atrium
spontaneous depolarization of the cardiac muscle can occur in the absence of nerve stimulation
action potentials are conducted from cell to cell via gap junctions
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. All three statements are correct: gap junctions electrically couple cardiac cells, the SA node sits in the right atrium, and the heart is autorhythmic (myogenic).

questions.q: What is the characteristic shape of an individual smooth muscle cell?
o: Cuboidal with a single flat side
questions.e: Smooth muscle cells are spindle shaped — thin and tapered at both ends — which distinguishes them from the cylindrical, multinucleated fibers of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: How many nuclei does a typical smooth muscle cell contain, and where is it located?
questions.e: Each smooth muscle cell has a single, centrally placed nucleus, unlike the many peripheral nuclei of skeletal muscle fibers.

questions.q: Which organelle is present in large numbers within smooth muscle cells, reflecting their metabolic activity?
questions.e: Smooth muscle cells contain lots of mitochondria, supporting the sustained, ATP-dependent tone these cells often maintain.

questions.q: The active tension developed in a muscle undergoing isometric contraction is attributed to
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Active tension comes from the contractile elements (actin-myosin cross-bridges); elastic elements contribute to passive tension.

questions.q: What are the thin filaments of smooth muscle composed of?
questions.e: The thin filaments are actin with tropomyosin. Notably, troponin — present in skeletal and cardiac muscle — is absent from smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT found in smooth muscle?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Smooth muscle contains actin, myosin, tropomyosin, and mitochondria, but it lacks troponin. Instead of the troponin–tropomyosin system used in skeletal/cardiac muscle, smooth muscle regulates contraction via calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) when bound to Ca²⁺.

questions.q: Dense bodies in smooth muscle serve a role functionally analogous to which skeletal muscle structure?
questions.e: Dense bodies are organizational sites for thick and thin filament attachment and are similar to the Z-lines of striated muscle.

questions.q: Which protein is characteristic of dense bodies in smooth muscle?
questions.e: Dense bodies contain the protein α-actinin, the same cross-linking protein family found at Z-lines in striated muscle.

questions.q: Which of the following acts as an ATPase during the contraction of skeletal muscle?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The myosin head has ATPase activity — it hydrolyzes ATP to power the cross-bridge cycle.

questions.q: Which proteins make up the non-contractile intermediate filaments of smooth muscle?
questions.e: Non-contractile intermediate filaments contain the proteins desmin or vimentin, which help relay contraction and shorten the whole cell.

questions.q: What are caveolae, and what is their proposed function in smooth muscle?
o: Plasma membrane invaginations that help bring in calcium for contraction
questions.e: Caveolae are numerous invaginations of the plasma membrane at the cell periphery, believed to help bring in the calcium needed for contraction.

questions.q: The triads in skeletal muscle are situated at the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Triads (T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the SR) are located at the junction of the A band and I band.

questions.q: How much sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is typically found in smooth muscle cells?
o: Very extensive, more than skeletal muscle
Identical in amount to skeletal muscle
Very little, compared with skeletal muscle
questions.e: Smooth muscle cells have very little sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is part of why caveolae and extracellular calcium entry are so important.

questions.q: Which type of junction between smooth muscle cells allows electrical coupling?
questions.e: Gap junctions are electrical junctions that allow ionic current (and therefore excitation) to spread directly between adjacent smooth muscle cells.

questions.q: Myosin light chain activation in smooth muscle is by
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), activated by Ca2+-calmodulin, phosphorylates the myosin light chain to permit cross-bridge cycling.

questions.q: Which of these statements about smooth muscle fibers is false?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Smooth muscle lacks troponin; it uses calmodulin to regulate contraction via myosin light chain kinase.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of multiunit smooth muscle?
questions.e: Multiunit smooth muscle is found in the walls of large blood vessels, in the eye (ciliary body), and at the base of hair follicles (piloerector muscles).

questions.q: Which one of these is not a characteristic of visceral smooth muscle?
o: The fibers behave as a syncytium
They do not have a stable membrane potential
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Visceral (single-unit) smooth muscle has sparse/low innervation density; cells are instead coupled by gap junctions and behave as a functional syncytium.

questions.q: Which statement about multiunit smooth muscle electrical coupling is correct?
o: Cells have extensive interconnecting bridges (gap junctions)
Cells share a common continuous membrane
Cells are connected only by tight junctions
questions.e: Multiunit smooth muscle cells have no interconnecting bridges, so excitation of one fiber does not readily spread to its neighbors.

questions.q: What is the resting membrane potential behavior of multiunit smooth muscle?
o: Fluctuates only in response to stretch
questions.e: In multiunit smooth muscle, the membrane potential is stable with no spontaneous depolarization.

questions.q: Visceral (unitary) smooth muscle is made up of fibers that are:
o: Bound together to form a single functional unit
questions.e: Visceral/unitary smooth muscle is made up of fibers bound together to form a single unit.

questions.q: Why do multiple fibers in visceral/unitary smooth muscle contract together as a unit?
o: Because they share one giant nucleus
Because impulses travel easily across gap junctions from cell to cell
Because each fiber is separately innervated
questions.e: Impulses travel easily across gap junctions from cell to cell in unitary smooth muscle, allowing coordinated contraction of the whole unit.

questions.q: What term describes the spontaneous, graded, rhythmical oscillations in membrane potential seen in some unitary smooth muscle?
questions.e: Self-excitable unitary smooth muscle generates spontaneous, graded, rhythmical oscillations in membrane potential called slow wave potentials, or pacemaker activity.

questions.q: Innervation density in visceral/unitary smooth muscle is generally:
questions.e: Visceral/unitary smooth muscle has low innervation density, relying instead on gap-junction spread of excitation between cells.

questions.q: The ability of smooth muscle to function over a wide range of length is called
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Plasticity allows smooth muscle to maintain tension despite changes in length (stress-relaxation response), letting it function well over a wide range of lengths (e.g. a filling bladder).

questions.q: The myogenic response of visceral/unitary smooth muscle refers to its tendency to:
questions.e: Unitary smooth muscle contracts when stretched — a myogenic response — independent of external nervous input.

questions.q: A tissue that shows spontaneous slow-wave pacemaker activity, low innervation density, and myogenic stretch responses is best classified as:
questions.e: These are all defining features of visceral/unitary smooth muscle, in contrast to the discrete, highly-innervated multiunit type.

questions.q: Depolarization of smooth muscle is by increase in intracellular
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Depolarization of smooth muscle is largely driven by Ca2+ influx (via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels), unlike skeletal/nerve where Na+ dominates.

questions.q: The function of the T-tubules in skeletal muscle is to
o: release Ca2+ into the cell from the ECF
transmit APs deep into the muscle cell
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that rapidly conduct the action potential from the cell surface deep into the interior of the muscle fiber, near the SR.

questions.q: How many distinct ways can intracellular calcium be increased in smooth muscle, according to the lecture?
questions.e: Intracellular calcium can be increased in three ways: voltage-gated (L-type) channel opening, calcium-induced calcium influx, and receptor-mediated calcium mobilization.

questions.q: Opening of which channel type occurs as a direct result of sarcolemmal depolarization?
questions.e: Depolarization of the sarcolemma opens voltage-gated calcium (L-type) channels, one of the three routes for raising intracellular Ca2+.

questions.q: In the ligand-gated Ca2+ channel pathway, where does the Ca2+ that enters the cytoplasm come from?
questions.e: Receptor occupancy opens Ca2+ channels in the sarcolemma, causing an influx of Ca2+ from the extracellular fluid (ECF).

questions.q: In the IP3-mediated pathway, where is Ca2+ released from?
o: The extracellular fluid via ligand-gated channels
The sarcoplasmic reticulum, via IP3 receptor channels
questions.e: Intracellular mobilization via IP3 results in Ca2+ release via inositol trisphosphate (IP3) receptor channels located in the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

questions.q: Which second messenger is generated alongside IP3 from the cleavage of PIP2 by phospholipase C?
questions.e: Phospholipase C (PLC) cleaves PIP2 into two products: IP3 and DAG (diacylglycerol).

questions.q: In the absence of troponin, what protein does free Ca2+ bind to initiate the smooth muscle contraction cascade?
questions.e: Free Ca2+ binds to calmodulin (CM) in a 4:1 ratio, substituting functionally for the troponin-based mechanism of striated muscle.

questions.q: Which protein binds tropomyosin/actin and blocks myosin binding in the relaxed state?
questions.e: Caldesmon binds to the tropomyosin/actin complex and blocks the binding of myosin to actin, keeping the muscle in the relaxed state until Ca2+ rises.

questions.q: What happens when Ca2+-calmodulin (CaCM) binds caldesmon?
o: Caldesmon is released from the tropomyosin/actin complex, permitting myosin binding
questions.e: Binding of CaCM to caldesmon releases caldesmon from the tropomyosin/actin complex, so myosin can now bind to the thin filament.

questions.q: Besides releasing caldesmon, what other key enzyme does the CaCM complex activate?
questions.e: The CaCM complex also activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), the central enzyme of smooth muscle contraction regulation.

questions.q: What does MLCK do, and what cofactor does it require?
o: Phosphorylates myosin light chains in the presence of ATP
questions.e: MLCK phosphorylates myosin light chains (MLC) in the presence of ATP, enabling crossbridge cycling to begin.

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for dephosphorylating myosin light chains, thereby causing smooth muscle relaxation?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes the phosphate group from myosin light chains, switching off cross-bridge cycling and causing smooth muscle to relax. This is the functional opposite of myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates (activates) the light chains to initiate contraction.

questions.q: What is the name given to the mechanism by which detached-rate-limited myosin heads hold force at low ATP cost?
questions.e: This is called the smooth muscle latch-bridge mechanism — myosin heads that stay attached hold force at the muscle ends.

questions.q: What is the physiological advantage of the latch-bridge mechanism?
o: It prevents smooth muscle from ever relaxing
It allows extremely fast, phasic contractions
It allows smooth muscle to maintain tone with minimal expenditure of ATP
It eliminates the need for calcium entirely
questions.e: The latch-bridge mechanism allows smooth muscle to maintain tone (force) with minimal expenditure of ATP — ideal for sustained tone in vessels and sphincters.

questions.q: Which best summarizes the overall Ca2+ signaling cascade for smooth muscle contraction?
o: Ca2+ → direct binding to myosin heads → immediate contraction
Ca2+ → troponin → tropomyosin shift → myosin binding
Ca2+ → inhibition of actin polymerization → relaxation
Ca2+ → calmodulin → caldesmon release + MLCK activation → MLC phosphorylation → crossbridge cycling
questions.e: The correct order is: Ca2+ binds calmodulin; CaCM releases caldesmon from actin/tropomyosin and activates MLCK; MLCK phosphorylates MLC; phosphorylated myosin engages in crossbridge cycling.

questions.q: A smooth, sustained contraction without any evidence of relaxation resulting from very rapid stimulation of the muscle is called
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Complete tetanus occurs when stimulation is fast enough that individual twitches fuse completely into one smooth, sustained contraction.

questions.q: Which transporter exchanges extracellular Na+ for intracellular Ca2+ to help extrude calcium?
questions.e: The 3Na+/Ca2+ exchanger uses the inward Na+ gradient to help extrude Ca2+ from the cell during relaxation.

questions.q: What is the length-tension behavior of smooth muscle when it is stretched?
o: A transient large force develops and then decays to a new constant level
Tension immediately reaches a stable plateau with no change over time
questions.e: When stretched, smooth muscle shows a transient large force (resistance to stretch) that decays to a new constant level within minutes — stress relaxation.

questions.q: Ca2+ extrusion associated with relaxation in smooth muscle is by
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Relaxation involves Ca2+ removal by the Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, the plasma membrane (sarcolemmal) Ca2+ ATPase, and the SR Ca2+ ATPase (SERCA) — all three contribute.

questions.q: Which organelle contributes to lowering cytosolic Ca2+ by actively pumping it back into internal stores?
questions.e: The sarcoplasmic reticulum reuptakes Ca2+ using a Ca2+ ATPase, one of the three mechanisms lowering cytosolic calcium during relaxation.

questions.q: "Stress relaxation" in smooth muscle refers to:
o: A property found only in skeletal muscle
An increase in tension over time without any stretch
A decrease in tension over time after a sudden stretch, at constant length
The process of caldesmon rebinding to actin
questions.e: Stress relaxation describes the transient large force after stretch that decays to a new, lower constant tension over minutes, at constant length.

questions.q: Which combination of pumps/exchangers work together to terminate the contractile signal in smooth muscle?
o: Na+/K+ ATPase and voltage-gated Ca2+ channels
3Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, sarcolemmal Ca2+ ATPase, and SR Ca2+ ATPase reuptake
questions.e: Together, the 3Na+/Ca2+ exchanger, sarcolemmal Ca2+ ATPase, and SR reuptake (via Ca2+ ATPase) lower intracellular Ca2+ and terminate contraction.

questions.q: What is the primary means by which cells communicate with one another?
o: Liberation of signal molecules such as hormones and neurotransmitters
questions.e: Cell communication occurs through the liberation of signal molecules (hormones, neurotransmitters) which bind to receptors and generate a response.

questions.q: The specialised site of transmission of information between two nerve cells is called the:
questions.e: The synapse is the site of transmission of information between cells.

questions.q: A typical synapse consists of a presynaptic cell, a postsynaptic cell, and:
questions.e: Every synapse has a presynaptic cell, postsynaptic cell, and the gap or cleft between them.

questions.q: Electrical synapses are found at:
questions.e: Electrical synapses occur at gap junctions, unlike chemical synapses which occur at synaptic clefts.

questions.q: The most common type of synapse in the nervous system is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Chemical synapses, using neurotransmitters, are by far the most common type in the nervous system.

questions.q: An action potential cannot cross the synaptic cleft between neurons directly because:
o: The postsynaptic membrane has no ion channels
Na+ channels are absent from the presynaptic membrane
The cleft is filled with myelin
Transmission there is chemical, not electrical, and the cleft interrupts electrical continuity
questions.e: Because transmission at a chemical synapse is mediated by neurotransmitter diffusion rather than direct current flow, an action potential cannot 'jump' across the cleft.

questions.q: The first step in the sequence of events at a chemical synapse is:
o: An action potential opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the nerve terminal
Ca2+ is pumped out of the presynaptic cell
questions.e: An action potential at the presynaptic neuron opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels concentrated in the nerve terminal — this is the first step.

questions.q: Entry of Ca2+ into the presynaptic terminal directly triggers:
o: Fusion of synaptic vesicles with the membrane and exocytosis of neurotransmitter
questions.e: Ca2+ causes synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic membrane, releasing neurotransmitter by exocytosis.

questions.q: A transient depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane produced by an excitatory neurotransmitter is called a(n):
questions.e: A transient depolarization causes an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP).

questions.q: Which of the following is not a possible drug effect on synaptic function?
o: Change the type of receptor found in the postsynaptic membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Drugs can affect synthesis, reuptake, inactivation, or receptor binding of a neurotransmitter, but they do not change the actual type of receptor expressed in the membrane.

questions.q: Neurotransmitter action at a synapse is normally terminated by all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Permanent, irreversible binding to the postsynaptic receptor
questions.e: Transmitter action is terminated by enzymatic breakdown or reuptake, not by permanent binding — this keeps the synapse from being permanently 'on'.

questions.q: Compared with chemical synapses, electrical synapses are generally:
o: Faster, and may transmit a signal in either direction
questions.e: Electrical synapses are rare and faster than chemical synapses, and often lack directional specificity.

questions.q: Triads are positioned near the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. A triad (one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum) is located at the junction between the A band and the I band in mammalian skeletal muscle — there are two triads per sarcomere, one at each A-I junction.

questions.q: Which one of these is false about electrical synapses?
o: They are faster than chemical synapses
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Electrical synapses are typically bidirectional (current can flow either way through the connexon channels), unlike chemical synapses which are unidirectional.

questions.q: An EPSP is typically produced by an increase in the conductance of which ions?
o: Na+ and K+, with the Na+ effect predominating
questions.e: EPSPs are produced by an increase in Na+ and K+ conductance, but the Na+ effect is greater.

questions.q: Why does the Na+ conductance dominate over K+ conductance during an EPSP even though both increase?
o: Because Na+ ions are heavier than K+ ions
Because K+ channels are absent from the membrane
Because the electrochemical gradient for Na+ is greater than for K+
Because K+ is actively pumped into the cell during an EPSP
questions.e: Na+ conductance dominates because the electrochemical gradient driving Na+ influx is greater than that for K+.

questions.q: An IPSP can be produced by:
o: Increased K+ efflux and/or increased Cl- influx
Opening of ligand-gated Na+ channels only
questions.e: IPSPs are produced by increased K+ efflux, increased Cl- influx, or closure of Na+/Ca2+ channels.

questions.q: The output of a neuron representing the algebraic sum of all excitatory and inhibitory potentials from its synapses is called:
questions.e: The GPSP is the sum of all excitatory and inhibitory potentials from all of a cell's synapses, forming its single output.

questions.q: If excitatory potentials on a neuron outweigh inhibitory potentials, the result is:
questions.e: More excitatory than inhibitory potentials produces facilitation; the reverse produces inhibition.

questions.q: Summation in which two action potentials arriving in quick succession from the SAME presynaptic neuron add together is called:
questions.e: When the second EPSP summates on the falling edge of the first from repeated firing, this is temporal summation.

questions.q: Summation that results from the cumulative effect of multiple synapses at multiple places on the neuron is designated
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Spatial summation refers to the combined effect of multiple simultaneous inputs at different synaptic sites on the neuron.

questions.q: Presynaptic inhibition is best described as:
o: Blockade of postsynaptic Na+ channels by curare
Postsynaptic hyperpolarization caused directly by GABA on the postsynaptic soma
Destruction of the presynaptic terminal by toxins
An axoaxonal inhibition of a stimulatory presynaptic neuron before it synapses
questions.e: Presynaptic inhibition is an axoaxonal inhibition of a stimulatory presynaptic neuron before it can synapse.

questions.q: In presynaptic inhibition, the transmitter released by the third (inhibiting) neuron mainly:
o: Inhibits voltage-gated Ca2+ channels on the presynaptic terminal
questions.e: The third neuron's transmitter inhibits voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, decreasing presynaptic Ca2+ influx and reducing transmitter release.

questions.q: IPSPs
o: are due to an increase in Na+ efflux
are due to a decrease in K+ efflux
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) are local hyperpolarizations (usually via Cl- influx or K+ efflux), moving the membrane further from threshold.

questions.q: GABA-B receptors typically mediate a slower, longer-lasting IPSP by activating:
questions.e: GABA-B activates voltage-gated K+ channels, producing a slower, longer IPSP.

questions.q: Which of these is classified as a neuroexciter (produces EPSPs)?
questions.e: Glutamate is a neuroexciter, along with ACh (in skeletal muscle), NE, E, dopamine, and aspartate.

questions.q: Which neurotransmitter is inhibitory (produces an IPSP) when acting on heart muscle, despite being excitatory elsewhere?
questions.e: ACh is a neuroinhibitor on heart muscle, though it is a neuroexciter at skeletal muscle.

questions.q: The neuromuscular (myoneural) junction is the synapse between:
o: A sensory neuron and a receptor cell
A gland cell and a neuron
A motor neuron terminal and the motor end plate of a muscle fibre
questions.e: The NMJ is the synapse of a motor neuron terminal with the motor end plate of a muscle fibre.

questions.q: At the neuromuscular junction, the terminal buttons are implanted in small invaginations of the sarcolemma called:
questions.e: The terminal buttons sit in invaginations called synaptic troughs, which are themselves thrown into junctional folds.

questions.q: The acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction are
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. The skeletal neuromuscular junction uses nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end-plate.

questions.q: Inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase can block neuromuscular transmission because
o: choline uptake is blocked by the presynaptic membrane
ACh is no longer secreted by the presynaptic membrane
ACh synthesis in the presynaptic membrane is inhibited
ACh is not degraded leading to a prolonged depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane
ACh is blocked from attaching to its receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Without acetylcholinesterase, ACh lingers in the synaptic cleft, causing persistent depolarization of the end-plate, which inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels and blocks further transmission.

questions.q: Nicotinic ACh receptors at the motor end plate, when bound by ACh, open channels permeable to:
questions.e: Binding of ACh to nicotinic receptors opens receptor-coupled Na+ and K+ channels.

questions.q: The transient depolarization of the motor end plate produced by ACh binding is called the:
questions.e: This local depolarization of the motor end plate is called the End-Plate Potential (EPP).

questions.q: The EPP triggers a full muscle action potential by acting as a local response that depolarizes adjacent regions via:
questions.e: The EPP serves as a current sink, electrotonically depolarizing adjacent muscle membrane until threshold is reached.

questions.q: After dissociating from nicotinic receptors, ACh is degraded by AChE into:
questions.e: AChE breaks ACh down into inactive choline and acetate.

questions.q: Most of the choline released from ACh breakdown at the NMJ is:
o: Returned to the presynaptic terminal via a Na+-choline cotransporter for ACh resynthesis
questions.e: Choline is returned to the presynaptic terminal by a Na+-choline cotransporter and combined with acetyl-CoA to resynthesize ACh.

questions.q: A Miniature End-Plate Potential (MEPP) results from:
o: Spontaneous release of a single quantum of ACh
questions.e: MEPPs result from spontaneous release of a single ACh quantum, producing about 0.5 mV depolarizations at ~1/second.

questions.q: An End-Plate Potential (EPP), unlike a MEPP, results from:
o: A nerve-impulse-evoked release of roughly 300 quanta of ACh
questions.e: The EPP results from a nerve impulse evoking a huge quantal release of about 300 quanta of ACh.

questions.q: Neuromuscular blocking agents (NMBAs) act by:
o: Interfering with neural transmission between motor neurons and skeletal muscle, causing paralysis
Blocking gap junctions in cardiac muscle
questions.e: NMBAs interfere with neuromuscular transmission and cause skeletal muscle paralysis.

questions.q: Tubocurarine is an example of a:
questions.e: Tubocurarine is a non-depolarizing blocker — a competitive ACh receptor antagonist at nicotinic receptors.

questions.q: The action of non-depolarizing blockers like tubocurarine can be reversed by:
questions.e: Non-depolarizing block is reversed by cholinesterase inhibitors, which raise ACh levels to out-compete the blocker.

questions.q: Succinylcholine is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that acts as a nicotinic receptor:
o: Agonist, causing prolonged depolarization and receptor inactivation
Partial agonist that blocks Ca2+ channels
questions.e: Succinylcholine is an ACh receptor agonist causing slow, prolonged depolarization so receptors remain inactive.

questions.q: Succinylcholine is more resistant to AChE and is instead degraded by:
questions.e: Succinylcholine is degraded by butyrylcholinesterase, a plasma cholinesterase, rather than AChE.

questions.q: Hemicholinium impairs neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Degrading ACh in the synaptic cleft
Blocking the Na+-choline transporter, depleting choline for ACh synthesis
questions.e: Hemicholiniums block the Na+-choline transporter, and prolonged use depletes choline needed for ACh synthesis.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Preventing vesicular docking and thus ACh release
questions.e: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release by preventing vesicular docking at the presynaptic membrane.

questions.q: Vesamicol impairs neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Blocking ACh transport into storage vesicles
questions.e: Vesamicol blocks ACh transport into storage vesicles, limiting how much ACh can be released.

questions.q: Black widow spider venom impairs neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Disrupting synaptic vesicles and depleting nerve terminals of ACh
questions.e: Black widow spider venom disrupts synaptic vesicles and depletes the nerve terminal of ACh.

questions.q: Junctional blockers that inhibit AChE cause accumulation of ACh at the junction, leading to:
o: Maintained end-plate depolarization, convulsions, then paralysis and death
Enhanced choline reuptake with no other effects
questions.e: AChE inhibition causes ACh accumulation and maintained depolarization, leading to convulsions, then paralysis and death — usually from paralysis of the diaphragm.

questions.q: Organophosphate insecticides and nerve gases act primarily by:
questions.e: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing ACh accumulation at cholinergic junctions.

questions.q: Myasthenia gravis results from
o: loss of Ach receptors in the end-plate membrane
insufficient Ach release from the presynaptic vesicles
excessive acetylcholinesterase that destroys the neurotransmitter
the motor neuron action potential being too small to shock the muscle membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies destroy/block nicotinic ACh receptors on the postsynaptic (end-plate) membrane, weakening neuromuscular transmission.

questions.q: Muscles most frequently affected in myasthenia gravis include those controlling:
o: Eye/eyelid movement, facial expression, and swallowing
questions.e: Muscles controlling the eyes/eyelids, facial expression, and swallowing are most frequently affected.

questions.q: Myasthenia gravis is commonly treated with anticholinesterase agents such as:
questions.e: Neostigmine and pyridostigmine allow ACh to accumulate in the cleft, improving transmission and muscle strength.

questions.q: The neuroeffector junction is the termination of a postganglionic autonomic nerve upon:
o: Smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and secretory tissue
questions.e: The neuroeffector junction is where postganglionic autonomic fibres terminate on smooth/cardiac muscle and glands.

questions.q: In the autonomic ground plexus, axons terminate as a series of swellings called:
questions.e: Axons lose part of their Schwann cell envelope and terminate as varicosities spaced 5–10 µm apart.

questions.q: The width of the junctional cleft at neuroeffector junctions:
o: Is identical to the electrical synapse gap junction width
Is always wider than at the NMJ
Varies widely, roughly 10 to 2000 nm, between organs
Is fixed at 20 nm in every organ
questions.e: The junctional cleft width at neuroeffector junctions varies considerably (10–2000 nm) between organs.

questions.q: Neurons at neuroeffector junctions may be cholinergic, adrenergic, purinergic, or:
questions.e: Autonomic neurons at neuroeffector junctions may be cholinergic, adrenergic, purinergic, or peptidergic.

questions.q: Cholinergic fibers, which liberate ACh, include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: Most sympathetic postganglionic fibres are adrenergic, not cholinergic — the exception is those innervating sweat glands and a few skeletal muscle blood vessels.

questions.q: The Ach receptors at the neuroeffector junction are
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. At autonomic neuroeffector junctions (e.g. postganglionic parasympathetic endings on organs), the ACh receptors are muscarinic.

questions.q: Stimulation of Gi-coupled muscarinic receptors typically:
o: Inhibits adenylate cyclase, decreasing cAMP production
Increases adenylate cyclase activity and raises cAMP
Has no effect on any second messenger
questions.e: Muscarinic receptors can stimulate Gi, which inhibits adenylate cyclase and decreases cAMP production.

questions.q: Adrenergic fibers secrete which transmitters?
questions.e: Fibres that secrete norepinephrine, dopamine, and epinephrine are called adrenergic fibres.

questions.q: Which enzymes are involved in norepinephrine handling and metabolism, as referenced in this topic?
questions.e: VMAT, MAO, and COMT are the enzymes/transporters referenced in norepinephrine synthesis, release, and metabolism.

questions.q: The two main classes of adrenergic receptors (adrenoceptors) are:
questions.e: Adrenoceptors are divided into alpha-adrenergic and beta-adrenergic receptors, each with subtypes.

questions.q: Norepinephrine generally has a higher affinity for which receptor type compared with epinephrine?
questions.e: NE has a higher affinity for alpha receptors, while epinephrine has a higher affinity for beta receptors.

questions.q: Denervation hypersensitivity refers to:
o: An immediate and total loss of receptor expression
Increased sensitivity to neurotransmitters or their agonists in effector organs after denervation
Decreased sensitivity to neurotransmitters after denervation
questions.e: Denervation hypersensitivity is increased sensitivity to neurotransmitters/agonists in effector organs following denervation.

questions.q: Denervation hypersensitivity typically develops how long after denervation?
o: Immediately and permanently, with no delay
questions.e: Denervation hypersensitivity develops roughly 7–14 days after denervation.

questions.q: A patient's blood sample is centrifuged and shows a hematocrit of 55%. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Hematocrit reflects the percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells (normal ~42-47%). A value of 55% indicates the red cell fraction is elevated relative to plasma, consistent with dehydration (reduced plasma volume) or polycythemia (increased red cell production).

questions.q: A sample of whole blood is allowed to clot fully, and the clot is removed. Compared to plasma, the remaining fluid (serum) is missing which components specifically?
o: Sodium, potassium and the other plasma electrolytes
Albumin and the globulin fractions of plasma protein
Fibrinogen and clotting factors V and VIII
Water along with the dissolved respiratory gases
questions.e: Serum is plasma minus the substances consumed during clot formation — specifically fibrinogen and clotting factors V and VIII — while albumin, globulins, and electrolytes remain unchanged.

questions.q: A patient with liver failure shows widespread tissue edema and low plasma oncotic pressure. Which plasma protein deficiency best explains this specific finding?
questions.e: Albumin, synthesized by the liver, is the primary contributor to plasma oncotic pressure, which keeps fluid within capillaries. Its deficiency (as in liver failure) allows fluid to leak into tissues, producing edema.

questions.q: A pathologist examining a blood smear notes red cells with an unusually high surface-area-to-volume ratio compared to a sphere of the same volume. Which structural feature of RBCs is responsible for this property?
questions.e: The biconcave disc shape of erythrocytes increases their surface-area-to-volume ratio compared to a sphere, and also allows the cell to deform and vary its shape as it squeezes through narrow capillaries without rupturing.

questions.q: A patient's MCV is measured at 105 fL and MCH at 22 pg. How would this red cell population be best described?
questions.e: MCV > 95 fL indicates macrocytosis (abnormally large cells); MCH < 25 pg indicates hypochromia (reduced hemoglobin content per cell). Together, this pattern (large but hemoglobin-poor cells) is classically seen in megaloblastic anemias from B12 or folate deficiency.

questions.q: Why does a reticulocyte count help distinguish between anemia due to blood loss versus anemia due to bone marrow failure?
o: Reticulocytes are only produced during hemorrhage, never otherwise
It reflects whether the marrow is able to respond
Reticulocytes appear only in polycythemia, never in anemia
Reticulocyte count bears no relation to marrow activity at all
questions.e: Since reticulocytes are the immediate precursor to mature RBCs, an elevated reticulocyte count signals that the marrow is actively compensating (e.g., after hemorrhage), whereas a low or normal count despite anemia suggests the marrow itself is failing to respond, as in aplastic anemia.

questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops anemia despite normal iron, B12, and folate levels, and a normal bone marrow biopsy. What is the most likely explanation?
o: Excessive RBC destruction in the spleen
Increased plasma volume diluting the red cells
Reduced erythropoietin production by the diseased kidneys
questions.e: Since 90-95% of erythropoietin is produced by the kidney, chronic kidney disease commonly leads to reduced erythropoietin secretion, and therefore reduced RBC production, despite adequate nutritional substrates and a structurally normal marrow.

questions.q: A patient with atrophic gastric mucosa and abnormal gastric juice develops a macrocytic anemia despite a diet adequate in vitamin B12. What is the most likely mechanism?
o: Increased hepcidin blocking B12 transport across the ileum
Excess folic acid competitively inhibiting B12 absorption
Deficiency of intrinsic factor from the parietal cells
A mutation in the transferrin gene reducing iron transport
questions.e: Pernicious anemia results not from inadequate dietary B12 but from defective absorption, due to loss of intrinsic factor (normally secreted by gastric parietal cells) — without intrinsic factor, B12 cannot be properly absorbed even when dietary intake is normal.

questions.q: A strict vegan with no B12 supplementation shows no signs of anemia even after 8 months. What is the most likely explanation, based on B12 physiology?
o: Vegan diets are naturally rich in B12
Folate fully substitutes for B12 in all of its reactions
Hepatic B12 stores last a year or more
B12 is not actually required for erythropoiesis at all
questions.e: The liver stores B12, and this store can last a year or longer even with inadequate intake or defective absorption — which is why B12 deficiency (dietary or pernicious) often takes a long time to become clinically apparent.

questions.q: A patient who underwent partial gastrectomy years ago now presents with iron deficiency, despite adequate dietary iron intake. What is the most likely link between the surgery and the deficiency?
o: Less gastric acid to convert Fe3+ to absorbable Fe2+
Excess vitamin C intake blocking iron absorption in the gut
Increased transferrin saturation resulting from the surgery
Loss of erythropoietin-secreting cells in the stomach
questions.e: Gastric acid converts dietary ferric iron (Fe3+) into the absorbable ferrous form (Fe2+). Partial gastrectomy reduces gastric acid secretion, impairing this conversion and reducing iron absorption even with adequate dietary intake.

questions.q: A patient with iron overload from repeated transfusions is found to have low serum apotransferrin production. What is the physiological rationale for this response?
o: Apotransferrin has no relationship to iron regulation
Low apotransferrin always indicates iron deficiency, never overload
Apotransferrin production is unrelated to liver function
The liver limits further iron transport into tissues
questions.e: When iron stores are full, the liver reduces apotransferrin production, limiting the transport form of iron available to carry more iron into tissues — a protective feedback response against iron overload.

questions.q: A menstruating woman and an adult man are compared for average daily iron loss. Which correctly reflects the physiological difference?
o: The man loses more, due to higher muscle myoglobin turnover
The woman loses considerably more, due to additional menstrual blood loss
Neither loses any iron under normal physiological conditions
They lose identical amounts, since both lose iron only through feces
questions.e: Men lose only about 0.1 mg of iron daily via feces, while menstruating women lose considerably more — an additional average of about 1.2 mg daily — due to menstrual blood loss, explaining why iron deficiency is more common in menstruating women.

questions.q: An elderly patient's red blood cells are found to be more fragile than normal and are being cleared prematurely by the spleen. What is the most direct underlying cause of this fragility as RBCs age toward the end of their 120-day lifespan?
o: Conversion of hemoglobin A to hemoglobin F
A steady increase in cell size as the cell ages
Gradual loss of hemoglobin from the cell
questions.e: As RBCs age, their metabolic processes (which generate the ATP needed to maintain the integrity of the cell membrane) weaken, making the cells progressively more fragile until they lyse when passing through small vascular spaces, especially in the spleen.

questions.q: A researcher compares HbA, HbA2, and HbF. Which correctly identifies the form present in the highest proportion in a healthy adult?
o: All three are present in exactly equal proportions
questions.e: HbA (α2β2) makes up about 96-98% of adult hemoglobin, making it by far the dominant form; HbA2 is a minor adult form (2-3%), and HbF is the dominant fetal form, present only in small amounts after infancy.

questions.q: A patient presents with fatigue, pallor, and a blood smear showing small, pale red cells. Which combination of findings would most strongly support iron-deficiency anemia specifically, rather than another cause of anemia?
o: Normal MCV, normal MCH, and low reticulocyte count
High MCV, low MCH, and normal ferritin
High MCV, normal MCH, and high serum ferritin
Low MCV, low MCH, and low serum ferritin
questions.e: Iron-deficiency anemia classically produces microcytic (low MCV), hypochromic (low MCH) red cells, together with depleted iron stores reflected as low serum ferritin — this combination together, not any single value alone, best supports the diagnosis.

questions.q: A patient with chronic hemolytic anemia (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis) would be expected to show which compensatory change in reticulocyte count?
o: Decreased, since hemolysis suppresses the marrow
Entirely absent, since the marrow shuts down
Unchanged, since hemolysis does not affect marrow output
questions.e: In hemolytic anemia, red cells are being destroyed faster than normal, so the bone marrow compensates by increasing red cell production — reflected as an elevated reticulocyte count, distinguishing this from anemias caused by underproduction.

questions.q: A patient living at high altitude for several months shows an elevated RBC count and hematocrit, with no underlying disease. What is the most likely physiological explanation?
o: Polycythemia rubra vera, a marrow malignancy
A right-to-left cardiac shunt causing mixing
Simple dehydration from the dry air at altitude
A normal adaptation to low tissue oxygenation
questions.e: High altitude exposes the body to chronically lower oxygen tension, triggering increased erythropoietin release and physiological polycythemia as a normal adaptive response to improve oxygen-carrying capacity — distinct from pathological causes like polycythemia rubra vera.

questions.q: A total WBC count of 2,000/µL (below the normal 4,000-11,000/µL range) would be classified as which condition, and what is the primary functional consequence?
o: Thrombocytopenia; an increased risk of bleeding
Leukocytosis; an increased risk of infection
Polycythemia; increased viscosity of the blood
questions.e: A WBC count below the normal range is leukopenia. Since the main function of leucocytes is defense against infection, a reduced count directly increases the patient's susceptibility to infection.

questions.q: A patient with a severe allergic reaction shows urticaria, rhinitis, and is at risk of anaphylactic shock. Which leucocyte type, through release of histamine and heparin, is most directly responsible for these hypersensitivity symptoms?
questions.e: Basophils release histamine and heparin and are specifically responsible for hypersensitivity reactions such as urticaria, rhinitis, and anaphylactic shock.

questions.q: A stool sample shows evidence of a parasitic infection, and blood work reveals a markedly elevated count of one specific granulocyte. Which cell type is most likely elevated, and why?
o: Monocytes, which respond only to viral infections
Basophils, which are the primary phagocytes of bacteria
Neutrophils, since they respond to all infections equally
questions.e: Eosinophils specifically attack parasites and are also involved in allergic reactions; their levels characteristically rise in parasitic infections and allergic conditions, distinguishing this pattern from a bacterial infection (which would favor neutrophilia).

questions.q: A wound develops visible pus. Which leucocyte is most directly responsible for pus formation, through its role in ingesting and killing bacteria?
questions.e: Neutrophils ingest and kill bacteria and are specifically responsible for the formation of pus, which consists largely of dead neutrophils and bacterial debris.

questions.q: Given that neutrophils have an average half-life in circulation of only about 6 hours, what does this imply about the bone marrow's production requirements?
o: The marrow must maintain very high daily neutrophil production to sustain normal blood levels
This short half-life has no bearing on marrow output
Marrow production of neutrophils can be minimal, since they last a long time
Neutrophils are never replaced once produced
questions.e: Because neutrophils survive only about 6 hours in circulation, the bone marrow must sustain a very high rate of daily production simply to maintain normal circulating levels — a much higher turnover demand than for longer-lived cells.

questions.q: A neutrophil squeezes between endothelial cells to leave the bloodstream and enter infected tissue. Which process describes this specific migration, and which chemical signal draws it toward the infection site?
questions.e: Diapedesis is the process of leucocyte migration through the endothelial wall into tissue, and chemotaxis is the process by which chemical signals from the infection site attract neutrophils toward it.

questions.q: Bacteria coated with IgG antibody are more readily engulfed by phagocytic cells. What is this antibody-coating process called, and what does it accomplish?
o: Diapedesis; it allows phagocytes to exit blood vessels
Opsonization; it marks the bacteria for more efficient phagocytosis
Agglutination; it clumps bacteria together for destruction
Chemotaxis; it attracts phagocytes from a distance
questions.e: Opsonization is the coating of bacteria (e.g., with IgG) that marks them for more efficient recognition and engulfment (phagocytosis) by immune cells — distinct from chemotaxis (attraction) or diapedesis (vessel exit).

questions.q: A patient's monocytes leave the bloodstream after about 72 hours in circulation and take up residence in the liver. What do these cells become, and what is the modern name for this network of resident phagocytes throughout the body?
o: Kupffer cells; part of the Tissue Macrophage System
Mast cells; part of the integumentary system
Osteoclasts; part of the skeletal system
Plasma cells; part of the lymphatic system
questions.e: Monocytes that migrate into the liver become Kupffer cells, one component of the broader Tissue Macrophage System (the modern name for what was historically called the Reticuloendothelial System), which also includes pulmonary alveolar macrophages and other tissue-resident phagocytes.

questions.q: A patient who recovered from a viral infection years ago mounts a rapid, strong antibody response upon re-exposure to the same virus. Which leucocyte property specifically explains this rapid recall response?
o: The immunological memory capacity of lymphocytes
The granular staining pattern of basophils
questions.e: Lymphocytes are responsible for both producing antibodies and for immunological memory — retaining the capacity to recognize and respond rapidly to a pathogen upon re-exposure, which explains the fast, strong secondary immune response.

questions.q: Which correctly distinguishes the roles of T-lymphocytes and B-lymphocytes in an immune response?
o: Only T-lymphocytes are involved in any immune response
Both cell types perform identical functions with full redundancy
T-lymphocytes handle transplant rejection and delayed allergic reactions; B-lymphocytes mediate antibody production
T-lymphocytes mediate antibody production directly; B-lymphocytes handle transplant rejection
questions.e: T-lymphocytes are responsible for reactions to foreign protein, delayed allergic reactions, and rejection of foreign tissue, while B-lymphocytes differentiate into plasma cells to mediate antibody (humoral) production — distinct, complementary roles.

questions.q: A type O blood donor and a type AB recipient are being matched for a transfusion. Based on ABO compatibility rules, why is this pairing generally considered safe?
o: Type O plasma contains no antibodies at all under any circumstance
Type O and type AB are chemically identical
Type O cells carry neither A nor B agglutinogen
AB recipients cannot safely receive any blood type
questions.e: Type O red cells lack both A and B agglutinogens, making them compatible with any ABO recipient (the 'universal donor'), and type AB recipients lack both anti-A and anti-B agglutinins, making them able to receive any ABO type (the 'universal recipient') — together explaining why this specific pairing is doubly safe.

questions.q: Damage to the ependymal cells would most likely affect the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Ependymal cells line the ventricles and, together with choroid plexus cells, are involved in producing/regulating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).

questions.q: An Rh-negative woman is pregnant with her second Rh-positive child, having not received anti-D prophylaxis after her first delivery. Why is this second pregnancy at higher risk than the first?
o: She was sensitized during the first delivery
The risk is identical regardless of prior pregnancies or prophylaxis
Rh-negative mothers cannot form antibodies against Rh-positive cells at all
Rh incompatibility only becomes relevant after the second pregnancy for unrelated reasons
questions.e: An Rh-negative mother has the capacity to form anti-D antibodies upon exposure to Rh-positive fetal cells (typically during a prior delivery). Without anti-D prophylaxis to prevent this sensitization, these maternal antibodies can cross the placenta in a subsequent Rh-positive pregnancy and cause hemolytic disease of the newborn.

questions.q: Anti-D immunoglobulin is administered to Rh-negative mothers during the postpartum period. What is the physiological rationale for giving this treatment specifically at this time?
o: It directly treats hemolytic disease in the current newborn
It has no specific timing requirement and works equally well at any point in life
It cures existing Rh sensitization from a previous pregnancy
It prevents her forming anti-D antibodies
questions.e: Anti-D immunoglobulin works by preventing the mother's immune system from mounting its own antibody response to fetal Rh-positive cells that entered her circulation during delivery — given postpartum, it protects against sensitization that would otherwise endanger future Rh-positive pregnancies.

questions.q: A patient with a severe vessel injury shows an initial, immediate reduction in blood flow to the area even before any platelet plug has formed. What accounts for this earliest hemostatic response?
o: Formation of a stable fibrin clot at the site
Local vasoconstriction of the vessel wall
Release of erythropoietin from the kidney
questions.e: The very first hemostatic response to vessel injury is local vasoconstriction — contraction of smooth muscle in the injured vessel wall — which reduces blood flow to the area even before platelet aggregation or clot formation has begun.

questions.q: A patient taking daily low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular protection is found to have reduced platelet aggregation. Through which specific mechanism does aspirin achieve this effect?
o: Increasing the activity of vitamin K
Blocking von Willebrand factor production entirely
questions.e: Aspirin reduces the formation of thromboxane A2 (normally produced from arachidonic acid in platelets), which lowers platelet aggregation — this is the specific mechanism behind aspirin's cardioprotective, anti-clotting effect.

questions.q: A patient with a deficiency of von Willebrand factor would be expected to show which specific defect in the hemostatic process?
o: Excessive, uncontrolled clot formation throughout the body
Inability to form the platelet plug
questions.e: Von Willebrand factor forms a bridge between the injured vessel wall (binding collagen) and the platelets (binding to them in turn), so its deficiency specifically impairs platelet plug formation, leading to a bleeding tendency.

questions.q: Prostacyclin, produced in the vessel wall, plays which role in the balance of hemostasis?
o: It promotes platelet aggregation throughout the vascular system
It directly activates the extrinsic clotting pathway
It has no functional role in hemostasis
questions.e: Prostacyclin opposes the action of thromboxane A2, inhibiting platelet aggregation in normal, uninjured vessels — this keeps platelet activation appropriately localized to the actual site of injury rather than spreading throughout the vasculature.

questions.q: A patient with a deep laceration to a large artery is brought to the emergency room with uncontrolled bleeding. Why do the body's natural hemostatic mechanisms often fail to stop bleeding from a large artery on their own, unlike a minor capillary cut?
