o: Platelets cannot function in arterial blood under any circumstance
Large arteries have no smooth muscle in their walls
Large arteries lack any hemostatic mechanisms at all
questions.e: Hemostatic mechanisms (vasoconstriction, platelet plug) are most effective for the smaller arterioles, capillaries, and venules; the high pressure and flow of larger arteries can overwhelm these natural mechanisms, which is why bleeding from a major artery typically requires external intervention.

questions.q: A laboratory test activates the clotting cascade using tissue thromboplastin added directly to a plasma sample. Which pathway is being specifically tested by this method?
o: Common pathway only, bypassing both intrinsic and extrinsic activation
questions.e: The extrinsic pathway is specifically activated by tissue factor (tissue thromboplastin), a protein external to the blood itself — this is the basis of the prothrombin time (PT) test, which uses added tissue thromboplastin to assess this pathway.

questions.q: A patient's blood is exposed to collagen from a damaged vessel wall, activating factors XII, XI, IX, and VIII in sequence. Which pathway does this describe, and how does its speed compare to the alternative pathway?
o: The fibrinolytic pathway, which dissolves rather than forms clots
The intrinsic pathway, which is slower
The extrinsic pathway, which is faster
The common pathway exclusively, with no distinction from the other pathways
questions.e: Exposure to collagen from vessel trauma activates the intrinsic pathway (factors XII, XI, IX, VIII), which is slower than the extrinsic pathway but is considered more physiologically important overall.

questions.q: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic clotting pathways ultimately converge on activation of which single factor, marking the start of the common pathway?
questions.e: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on the activation of Factor X to Xa, which marks the beginning of the common pathway, ultimately leading to thrombin generation and fibrin formation.

questions.q: A patient's blood fails to form a stable clot despite normal platelet counts and normal levels of factors II, V, VII-XII. Which specific factor deficiency would most directly explain a failure to STABILIZE the fibrin mesh once formed?
questions.e: Factor XIII is specifically responsible for stabilizing the fibrin mesh once it has formed from fibrinogen; its deficiency would allow initial clot formation but result in an unstable, poorly cross-linked clot.

questions.q: A patient with severe liver disease shows prolonged bleeding. Given that the liver is central to both bile production and plasma protein synthesis, which two distinct mechanisms could explain the bleeding tendency?
o: Reduced vitamin K absorption AND reduced synthesis of clotting factors by the diseased liver
Neither mechanism is relevant; liver disease has no effect on clotting
Only reduced vitamin K absorption, since the liver does not synthesize clotting factors
Only reduced synthesis of clotting factors, since bile is unrelated to clotting
questions.e: Liver disease can impair hemostasis through two separate mechanisms: reduced bile production impairs fat-soluble vitamin K absorption (needed for several clotting factors), and the diseased liver itself has reduced capacity to synthesize plasma clotting proteins directly.

questions.q: A young male patient with a family history on his mother's side of excessive bleeding after minor cuts is diagnosed with a deficiency of Factor VIII. Which inheritance pattern best explains why this condition is much more common in males?
o: Autosomal recessive inheritance with no sex bias
questions.e: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII deficiency) follows X-linked inheritance, since the gene is located on the X chromosome — this explains why it is much more common in males (who have only one X chromosome) and why it often runs through the maternal line.

questions.q: A patient develops a deep vein thrombosis after a long-haul flight involving prolonged immobility. Which combination of factors most directly explains this increased clotting risk?
o: Increased erythropoietin secretion during the flight
Increased blood pH and decreased platelet count
questions.e: Thrombus formation is particularly favored by sluggish blood flow, which is especially relevant in veins during conditions like prolonged immobility (long flights, post-operative bed rest) — stagnant flow allows activated clotting factors to accumulate locally rather than being washed away.

questions.q: A thrombus that has formed in a deep leg vein breaks free and travels through the circulation, eventually lodging in a pulmonary vessel. What is this traveling clot fragment called, and what serious condition can it cause in this scenario?
o: A thrombus; causing a cerebral stroke
questions.e: Once a thrombus breaks away and travels through the circulation, it is called an embolus. An embolus that lodges in a pulmonary vessel after originating in a deep vein causes a pulmonary embolism, a potentially life-threatening condition.

questions.q: A patient on heparin therapy develops excessive bleeding, and the clinical team administers protamine. What is the mechanism by which protamine reverses heparin's anticoagulant effect?
o: Protamine directly synthesizes new clotting factors
questions.e: Protamine binds to and inactivates heparin, preventing heparin from enhancing antithrombin III's ability to inhibit clotting factors — this is the specific mechanism used clinically to reverse heparin overdose.

questions.q: Warfarin is prescribed to a patient at risk of thrombosis. Given its mechanism of action, which vitamin-dependent clotting factors would be most directly reduced by this therapy?
o: Factors II, VII, IX and X
Only platelet-derived factors, since warfarin does not affect plasma proteins
Only Factor VIII, since warfarin is specific to hemophilia-related factors
All clotting factors equally, since warfarin has no specificity
questions.e: Warfarin works by inhibiting the action of vitamin K, which is required for the synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X (as well as proteins C and S) — these are the factors most directly reduced by warfarin therapy.

questions.q: A patient presents with an acute ischemic stroke due to a fresh clot blocking a cerebral vessel. Streptokinase is administered. What is the rationale for using this specific drug in this acute scenario, as opposed to heparin or warfarin?
o: Streptokinase is used only to reduce platelet counts
Streptokinase works identically to heparin, with no meaningful difference
It dissolves the clot already formed
Streptokinase directly replaces the missing clotting factors
questions.e: Streptokinase is a thrombolytic agent that actively breaks down an already-formed clot, making it appropriate for acute clot-related emergencies like ischemic stroke — unlike heparin or warfarin, which only prevent further clot formation without dissolving existing clots.

questions.q: Antithrombin III circulates in the blood as a natural anticoagulant. Which clotting factors does it directly inhibit by binding to them?
o: Factors IX, X, XI and XIIa
questions.e: Antithrombin III is a circulating protease inhibitor that binds to and blocks the activity of factors IX, X, XI, and the active form of XII, with this inhibitory activity greatly enhanced by heparin.

questions.q: Protein C, activated with the help of endothelial thrombomodulin, contributes to anticoagulation through which additional mechanism, beyond its direct anticoagulant activity?
o: It converts fibrinogen directly into fibrin
It has no role beyond direct clotting factor inhibition
questions.e: Beyond acting as a direct anticoagulant, activated Protein C also inactivates inhibitors of tissue plasminogen activator, which indirectly promotes the fibrinolytic system's ability to break down clots that have already formed.

questions.q: A clinician orders both a bleeding time and a clotting time on a patient with unexplained bruising. The bleeding time is prolonged but the clotting time is normal. Which category of disorder does this pattern most strongly suggest?
o: Normal clotting cascade function throughout, ruling out any disorder
A deficiency isolated to Factor XII alone
A deficiency of intrinsic pathway clotting factors (e.g., factor IX)
questions.e: Bleeding time specifically reflects platelet function, vascular integrity, and the extrinsic pathway, while clotting time reflects the intrinsic and common pathways. A prolonged bleeding time with a normal clotting time points toward a platelet, vascular, or extrinsic pathway problem rather than an intrinsic pathway factor deficiency.

questions.q: Blood collected into a tube containing sodium citrate does not clot in the tube. What is the mechanism by which citrate prevents clotting in this collection tube?
o: Citrate activates the fibrinolytic system to dissolve any clot immediately
questions.e: Citrate (like oxalate) works by chelating (binding and removing) free calcium ions. Since calcium (Factor IV) is an essential cofactor at multiple steps of the clotting cascade, its removal prevents the sample from clotting in the collection tube.

questions.q: A prothrombin time (PT) test is performed by adding calcium and tissue thromboplastin back to an oxalated plasma sample. What does a significantly prolonged PT result most directly suggest?
o: A deficiency in intrinsic pathway factors exclusively
An excess of circulating red blood cells
Deficiency of extrinsic or common pathway factors
questions.e: Since the PT test specifically initiates the extrinsic pathway (via added tissue thromboplastin) before proceeding through the common pathway, a prolonged PT points toward a deficiency in prothrombin or other extrinsic/common pathway factors.

questions.q: Why is bleeding time from a minor wound normally shorter than the formal laboratory clotting time measured on a blood sample?
o: Because minor wounds never actually stop bleeding without medical intervention
Because laboratory clotting time does not involve any clotting factors
Because bleeding time and clotting time measure the exact same process and should always be equal
Vasoconstriction and the platelet plug act faster
questions.e: Bleeding from a minor wound typically stops through rapid vasoconstriction and platelet plug formation, occurring before a fully formed, stable fibrin clot (which is what formal clotting time measures) has developed — explaining why bleeding time is normally shorter than clotting time.

questions.q: A patient with thrombocytopenic purpura and a patient with thromboasthenic purpura both present with easy bruising, but for different underlying reasons. Which best distinguishes the two conditions?
o: Thrombocytopenic purpura involves excess platelets; thromboasthenic purpura involves a complete absence of platelets
Both conditions involve identical platelet counts and function
Neither condition involves platelets at all
Thrombocytopenic purpura involves low platelet numbers; thromboasthenic purpura involves normal platelet numbers that are functionally abnormal
questions.e: Thrombocytopenic purpura is caused by an abnormally LOW platelet count, while thromboasthenic purpura involves platelets present in normal numbers but functioning abnormally — both produce similar bruising symptoms through different underlying platelet defects.

questions.q: A boy accidentally ate mushroom containing muscarine. What symptoms would you expect to observe?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Muscarine over-stimulates muscarinic receptors, producing classic parasympathomimetic effects: diarrhea, salivation, bradycardia (low heart rate), and sweating — all of the above.

questions.q: If a man's plasma volume is 3 litres and hematocrit is 0.40, what will his total blood volume be?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Blood volume = Plasma volume ÷ (1 − hematocrit) = 3 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = 3 ÷ 0.6 = 5 l.

questions.q: A researcher wants to selectively measure only the red cell mass of a patient's blood, independent of plasma volume. Which single measurement most directly reflects this?
questions.e: Hematocrit (packed cell volume) specifically measures the fraction of total blood volume made up of red cells, making it the direct measurement of red cell mass relative to the sample, independent of plasma protein or leucocyte content.

questions.q: Which of the following would be expected to increase MCHC (Mean Corpuscular Hemoglobin Concentration) without necessarily changing MCV?
o: An increase in the white cell count
A decrease in total blood volume alone
More hemoglobin packed into each cell
An increase in the number of red cells alone
questions.e: MCHC specifically reflects the concentration of hemoglobin within each red cell (Hb/Hematocrit), which can change based on how densely hemoglobin is packed into cells, independent of whether the cells themselves are larger or smaller (which would affect MCV instead).

questions.q: A patient with chronic lung disease causing ventilation/perfusion mismatch develops secondary polycythemia. What is the physiological chain of events leading to this outcome?
o: Lung disease directly increases bone marrow cellularity with no hormonal intermediary
Polycythemia in this context is unrelated to oxygen levels
Reduced blood pH alone causes polycythemia regardless of oxygen status
questions.e: Ventilation/perfusion mismatch impairs oxygen delivery to tissues; this reduced tissue oxygenation is a recognized trigger for increased erythropoietin secretion, which in turn stimulates increased red cell production, producing secondary polycythemia.

questions.q: A patient with cardiac failure shows reduced blood flow to the kidneys as a downstream effect. Which erythropoietic consequence would this be expected to trigger, based on the known triggers for erythropoietin release?
o: No effect on erythropoiesis, since cardiac failure is unrelated to red cell production
Decreased erythropoietin release specifically due to reduced blood flow
questions.e: Reduced blood flow (as in cardiac failure) is one of the recognized conditions causing reduced tissue oxygenation, including in the kidney — since the kidney is the primary source of erythropoietin, this reduced renal oxygenation would be expected to trigger increased erythropoietin release, stimulating compensatory red cell production.

questions.q: In the plasma membrane, carbohydrates:
o: Always face the lumen of the cell
Always face inward, towards the non-polar portion of the membrane
Always face outward, towards extracellular space
Are directed to all sides in the membrane
questions.e: Membrane carbohydrates are attached to lipids (glycolipids) or proteins (glycoproteins) exclusively on the outer leaflet, forming the glycocalyx. This layer faces the extracellular space and is involved in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection — it never faces the cytoplasmic side.

questions.q: Which of the following is a primary messenger?
questions.e: A primary (first) messenger is the extracellular signal — usually a hormone or neurotransmitter — that binds a cell-surface receptor. TSH fits this role. cAMP, calmodulin, and PLC-generated products (IP₃/DAG) are all second messengers generated inside the cell after receptor activation.

questions.q: Regarding the cell membrane, which of the following is FALSE?
o: The membrane's fluidity is increased by unsaturated fatty acid tails in the phospholipids
The proteins of the cell membrane function as channels, carriers, enzymes and receptors
About 50% of the cell membrane is made up of protein
The hydrophilic part of the cell membrane is at the interior side of the cell membrane
questions.e: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: the hydrophilic (polar) heads face outward on BOTH surfaces (toward the extracellular fluid and toward the cytoplasm), while the hydrophobic tails point inward, forming the membrane's non-polar core. Saying the hydrophilic part is only 'at the interior side' is incorrect — that describes the hydrophobic tails, not the heads. (Note: option D was left incomplete in the original paper and has been reconstructed here as a true statement to complete the option set.)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT found in smooth muscle?
questions.e: Smooth muscle contains actin, myosin, tropomyosin, and mitochondria, but it lacks troponin. Instead of the troponin–tropomyosin system used in skeletal/cardiac muscle, smooth muscle regulates contraction via calmodulin, which activates myosin light chain kinase (MLCK) when bound to Ca²⁺.

questions.q: The main function of nociceptors is to sense:
questions.e: Nociceptors are free nerve endings specialized to detect noxious (potentially damaging) stimuli — mechanical, thermal, or chemical — and transmit signals that are perceived as pain.

questions.q: What functions as the skeletal muscle contractile unit?
questions.e: The sarcomere — the region between two adjacent Z-lines — is the basic contractile (functional) unit of skeletal muscle. Myofibrils are made up of many sarcomeres in series; the I band and H band are just sub-regions within a sarcomere.

questions.q: The force of a tetanic contraction is greater than that of a single twitch contraction because:
o: Twitch contractions only involve fast-twitch (Type II) fibers, which are inherently weaker
Tetany results from one large stimulus, whereas a twitch results from repeated small stimuli
Tetanic stimulation recruits a larger number of individual muscle fibers than a twitch does
Successive stimuli arrive before the muscle can fully relax, so individual contractions summate while Ca²⁺ stays elevated, allowing continuous cross-bridge cycling
questions.e: In a single twitch, the muscle has time to relax fully between the stimulus and the next possible contraction. In tetanus, stimuli arrive in rapid succession — faster than the relaxation time — so cytosolic Ca²⁺ remains persistently elevated and successive twitches mechanically summate, producing a smooth, sustained contraction with much greater force than any single twitch. (This was an open-ended question in the original paper; it has been converted into a single-best-answer item here.)

questions.q: Regarding excitation–contraction coupling, which of the following is correct?
o: The muscle action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules
The Ca²⁺ released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to tropomyosin
In the resting state, tropomyosin (not troponin itself) sterically blocks the myosin-binding site on actin
Relaxation occurs when Ca²⁺ is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA
questions.e: Excitation–contraction coupling begins with the action potential spreading along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules, which triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Note: Ca²⁺ actually binds troponin (not tropomyosin) which then shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding site — so the classic textbook statement in option B is a common trap. Option A is the accurate first step of the process.

questions.q: T-tubules are contiguous with which membrane system?
questions.e: T-tubules (transverse tubules) are tube-like invaginations of the sarcolemma (the muscle cell membrane) that dive deep into the fiber, allowing the action potential to reach the interior of the cell rapidly and uniformly.

questions.q: Triads are positioned near the:
questions.e: A triad (one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum) is located at the junction between the A band and the I band in mammalian skeletal muscle — there are two triads per sarcomere, one at each A-I junction.

questions.q: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for dephosphorylating myosin light chains, thereby causing smooth muscle relaxation?
questions.e: Myosin light chain phosphatase (MLCP) removes the phosphate group from myosin light chains, switching off cross-bridge cycling and causing smooth muscle to relax. This is the functional opposite of myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), which phosphorylates (activates) the light chains to initiate contraction.

questions.q: At what point in the ventricular action potential is the membrane most permeable to Ca²⁺?
questions.e: The plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is sustained by inward Ca²⁺ current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels, which balances outward K⁺ current — this is when Ca²⁺ permeability is at its highest, and it's also what triggers Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release for contraction.

questions.q: The upstroke of the SA nodal action potential is produced by opening of a channel that is:
o: Equally permeable to K⁺ and Na⁺
questions.e: Unlike ventricular myocytes, SA nodal cells lack significant fast Na⁺ channel activity. Their action potential upstroke (phase 0) is instead driven by the opening of L-type Ca²⁺ channels, producing a comparatively slower, Ca²⁺-dependent depolarization.

questions.q: The channel responsible for the initiation of spontaneous depolarization in phase 4 of the SA node cell exhibits which of the following properties?
o: It is opened by vagal nerve stimulation
It is opened by membrane depolarization
questions.e: This describes the funny current (Iꜰ) channel — unusual because it is activated by hyperpolarization/repolarization (not depolarization) at the end of the previous action potential, and it conducts a net inward, depolarizing current that is primarily carried by Na⁺. Vagal stimulation (ACh) actually slows it down, and norepinephrine enhances (not closes) it — both B, C and E describe the opposite of what actually happens.

questions.q: If 30 mg of glucose is added to an unknown volume of distilled water and the final concentration of glucose after mixing is 0.10 mg/ml, then the volume of solvent is?
questions.e: Volume = mass ÷ concentration = 30 mg ÷ 0.10 mg/ml = 300 ml.

questions.q: Which one of these cannot be measured directly using a marker?
questions.e: There is no marker that distributes only in the interstitial space; it is calculated indirectly as ECF volume minus plasma volume.

questions.q: If a man's plasma volume is 3 litres and hematocrit is 0.40, what will his total blood volume be?
questions.e: Blood volume = Plasma volume ÷ (1 − hematocrit) = 3 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = 3 ÷ 0.6 = 5 l.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about plasma membranes?
o: It is involved in cell to cell communication
questions.e: The lipid bilayer is actually poorly permeable to ions; ions cross mainly through specific channels/transporters, not by free diffusion.

questions.q: The least phospholipids present in the plasma membranes are the
questions.e: Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant membrane phospholipid; phosphatidylinositol is present in the smallest amount, though it is functionally important as a second-messenger precursor.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about transmembrane proteins?
o: They are embedded in the lipid bilayer
They can be removed by alkaline solutions
They have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic ends
questions.e: Integral/transmembrane proteins span the bilayer and need detergents to be removed. Alkaline (or high salt) solutions only strip loosely-associated peripheral proteins.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about Fick's first law of diffusion?
o: Diffusion rate is directly proportional to diffusion coefficient
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to concentration gradient of the substance across the membrane
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to surface area of the membrane
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to permeability of the membrane to the substance
Diffusion rate is directly proportional to thickness of the membrane
questions.e: Fick's law: rate is inversely proportional to membrane thickness (the thicker the membrane, the slower the diffusion) — not directly proportional.

questions.q: Membrane junctions that allow nutrients or ions to flow from cell to cell are
questions.e: Gap junctions are made of connexons that form direct cytoplasmic channels between adjacent cells, allowing ions/small molecules to pass.

questions.q: The uptake of particulate matter by a cell is
questions.e: Phagocytosis ('cell eating') is uptake of large particulate matter; pinocytosis is uptake of fluid/solutes.

questions.q: Uptake of molecules by caveolae is termed
questions.e: Potocytosis is the specific term for molecule uptake via caveolae (flask-shaped membrane invaginations rich in caveolin).

questions.q: ____ utilize aquaporins to rapidly move across cellular membranes
questions.e: Aquaporins are water-channel proteins that allow rapid, selective movement of water across the membrane.

questions.q: Two of these organ systems bear the major responsibility for ensuring homeostasis: 1. Nervous system 2. Digestive system 3. Reproductive system 4. Cardiovascular system 5. Endocrine system
questions.e: The nervous system and endocrine system are the two major regulatory systems that maintain homeostasis, communicating via electrical signals and hormones respectively.

questions.q: Which one of these is not controlled by negative feedback mechanism?
questions.e: The pre-ovulatory LH surge is a classic example of positive feedback — rising estrogen further stimulates LH release rather than inhibiting it.

questions.q: The mechanism in which a response is generated in anticipation of a change in a control variable is
questions.e: Feedforward control anticipates a change and initiates a response before the change actually occurs (e.g. salivation at the sight of food).

questions.q: Which one of these does not act by a cytoplasmic receptor?
questions.e: Acetylcholine is hydrophilic and binds membrane-bound receptors (nicotinic/muscarinic); steroid hormones and NO act via intracellular/cytoplasmic receptors.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a second messenger?
questions.e: RGS (Regulator of G-protein Signaling) is a protein that accelerates GTP hydrolysis on G-alpha subunits — it is a signalling regulator, not a second messenger.

questions.q: The enzyme responsible for conversion of ATP to cAMP is
questions.e: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP; phosphodiesterase later breaks cAMP down, terminating the signal.

questions.q: When a catecholamine binds to a membrane bound receptor, the
o: hormone-receptor complex moves into the nucleus
hormone-receptor complex moves into the cytoplasm
second messengers appear in the cytoplasm
questions.e: Catecholamines act via membrane G-protein-coupled receptors, triggering intracellular second messengers (e.g. cAMP, IP3) rather than the complex itself entering the cell.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a catalytic receptor?
questions.e: Adenylate (adenylyl) cyclase is an effector enzyme activated downstream of a G-protein-coupled receptor — it is not itself a catalytic (enzyme-linked) receptor.

questions.q: When thyroxin binds to its receptor to form a hormone-receptor complex,
questions.e: Thyroxine binds an intracellular/nuclear receptor; the hormone-receptor complex acts directly on DNA to initiate gene transcription.

questions.q: Neurotransmitters are stored in
questions.e: Neurotransmitters are packaged and stored inside synaptic vesicles within the axon terminal (terminal button).

questions.q: Neurons that secrete acetylcholine as their main transmitter are
questions.e: Neurons that release acetylcholine are termed cholinergic.

questions.q: Neurones in the CNS are myelinated by
questions.e: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons); Schwann cells perform this role in the PNS.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: The glial cells that form the blood-brain barrier are the
questions.e: Astrocyte end-feet surround brain capillaries and induce/maintain the tight junctions of the blood-brain barrier.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Damage to the ependymal cells would most likely affect the
questions.e: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and, together with choroid plexus cells, are involved in producing/regulating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Which of these does not contribute to the generation of the resting membrane potential of a neuron?
o: Active transport of Na+ out of the cell
Na+ influx through voltage gated Na+ channels
Active transport of K+ into the cell
questions.e: Voltage-gated Na+ channels are closed at rest and only open during depolarization — they do not contribute to the resting potential.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: The equilibrium potential of an ion can be calculated using the
questions.e: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a single ion based on its concentration gradient.

questions.q: The resting membrane potential of a neuron can be calculated using the
questions.e: The GHK equation accounts for the relative permeabilities and concentrations of multiple ions (K+, Na+, Cl−) to give the overall resting membrane potential.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Which one of these is not a characteristic of graded potentials?
questions.e: Refractory periods are a feature of action potentials (due to Na+ channel inactivation), not graded potentials, which can summate freely without a refractory period.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Which of these is not true about the neuronal action potential?
questions.e: An action potential is not 'always depolarizing' — it involves a depolarization phase followed by repolarization (and often after-hyperpolarization). Also, action potentials do not summate (feature b in the list is the false one; note option d 'It summates' is also false, but the classically tested false statement here is 'always depolarizing').
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: The repolarization phase of the action potential is as a result of
o: opening of voltage gated K+ channels
closing of voltage gated Na+ channels
inactivation of voltage gated Na+ channels
questions.e: Repolarization results from both inactivation of Na+ channels (stopping further depolarization) and opening of voltage-gated K+ channels (driving K+ efflux).
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Which of these sensations is not monitored by interoceptors?
questions.e: Vision is a special exteroceptive/special sense; interoceptors monitor the internal state of the body (thirst, nausea, blood pressure, fatigue).

questions.q: Which one of these does not belong to the special senses?
questions.e: Nociception (pain) is a general (somatic) sense detected by receptors distributed throughout the body, not a special sense.

questions.q: The adequate stimulus of nociceptors is
questions.e: Nociceptors respond to noxious/tissue-damaging stimuli, generating the sensation of pain — the best-fit answer among the options given.

questions.q: The connective tissue that encloses the sarcolemma of an individual muscle fiber is called
questions.e: Endomysium surrounds individual muscle fibers; perimysium surrounds fascicles (bundles); epimysium surrounds the whole muscle.

questions.q: The function of the T-tubules in skeletal muscle is to
o: transmit APs deep into the muscle cell
release Ca2+ into the cell from the ECF
questions.e: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that rapidly conduct the action potential from the cell surface deep into the interior of the muscle fiber, near the SR.

questions.q: The triads in skeletal muscle are situated at the
questions.e: Triads (T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the SR) are located at the junction of the A band and I band.

questions.q: At rest, the tropomyosin molecule is held in place by
questions.e: Troponin binds tropomyosin and, at rest (low Ca2+), holds it over the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Myosin binding sites on the actin filament are exposed after
questions.e: Ca2+ binding to troponin C causes a conformational change that shifts tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: The voltage-dependent calcium channels found in the membrane of the T tubules are called
questions.e: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are the voltage sensors/Ca2+ channels in the T-tubule membrane that mechanically couple to ryanodine receptors on the SR.

questions.q: Which of the following acts as an ATPase during the contraction of skeletal muscle?
questions.e: The myosin head has ATPase activity — it hydrolyzes ATP to power the cross-bridge cycle.

questions.q: The most important factor in decreasing the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in skeletal muscle is
o: active transport of Ca2+ across the sarcolemma
diffusion of Ca2+ out of the cell
active transport of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
active transport of Ca2+ into the synaptic cleft
diffusion of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm reticulum
questions.e: The SERCA pump actively transports Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is the primary mechanism lowering cytosolic Ca2+ and allowing relaxation.

questions.q: Alactic anaerobic ATP generation by skeletal muscle is by
questions.e: The phosphagen (creatine phosphate/ATP-PCr) system generates ATP anaerobically without producing lactate — hence 'alactic anaerobic'.

questions.q: Which of these is not true during oxidative phosphorylation
questions.e: Pyruvic acid is produced during glycolysis and consumed (converted to Acetyl-CoA) before oxidative phosphorylation — it is not produced during this process.

questions.q: The type of contraction in which the muscle fiber does not shorten is called
questions.e: Isometric contraction generates tension without a change in muscle length.

questions.q: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates is called
questions.e: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates.

questions.q: The rapid rise and fall in force produced by a muscle fiber after a single action potential is
questions.e: A single action potential produces a single twitch — a brief rise and fall in tension.

questions.q: Fast fibers
questions.e: Fast (glycolytic) fibers fatigue quickly (low fatigue resistance) because they rely mainly on anaerobic glycolysis and have fewer mitochondria, less myoglobin, and less vascularization than slow fibers.

questions.q: A smooth, sustained contraction without any evidence of relaxation resulting from very rapid stimulation of the muscle is called
questions.e: Complete tetanus occurs when stimulation is fast enough that individual twitches fuse completely into one smooth, sustained contraction.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle at rest, the myosin binding sites on actin filaments are blocked by
questions.e: Tropomyosin physically covers the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest; troponin regulates the position of tropomyosin.

questions.q: Which of these statements about smooth muscle fibers is false?
questions.e: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; it uses calmodulin to regulate contraction via myosin light chain kinase.

questions.q: The ability of smooth muscle to function over a wide range of length is called
questions.e: Plasticity allows smooth muscle to maintain tension despite changes in length (stress-relaxation response), letting it function well over a wide range of lengths (e.g. a filling bladder).

questions.q: Which one of these is not a characteristic of visceral smooth muscle?
o: The fibers behave as a syncytium
They do not have a stable membrane potential
questions.e: Visceral (single-unit) smooth muscle has sparse/low innervation density; cells are instead coupled by gap junctions and behave as a functional syncytium.

questions.q: Myosin light chain activation in smooth muscle is by
questions.e: Myosin light chain kinase (MLCK), activated by Ca2+-calmodulin, phosphorylates the myosin light chain to permit cross-bridge cycling.

questions.q: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the
questions.e: The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous depolarization and normally sets the heart rate.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle is false?
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is autorhythmic/myogenic — it generates its own action potentials at the SA node and does not require neural stimulation to contract (though the ANS modulates rate and force).

questions.q: The heart is innervated by
questions.e: The heart receives dual innervation — vagal (parasympathetic) fibers slow it down and sympathetic fibers speed it up / increase its force.

questions.q: Tetanic muscle contractions do not occur in a normal cardiac muscle because
o: the refractory period lasts until the muscle relaxes
the refractory period ends before the muscle reaches peak tension
cardiac muscle contract on its own
questions.e: Cardiac muscle has a long absolute refractory period that lasts almost as long as the contraction itself, preventing summation and tetanus — essential for the heart's pumping cycle.

questions.q: In the heart
o: sympathetic stimulation decreases time available for ventricular filling
sympathetic stimulation increases its force of contraction
questions.e: All are true: vagal stimulation slows the heart, sympathetic stimulation shortens diastole (reducing filling time) and increases contractile force (positive inotropy).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about cardiac muscle is true?
o: Ca2+ are not released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
About half the Ca2+ required for contraction comes from outside the cell
Ca2+ play no role in the process of contraction
Ca2+ plays an important role in repolarization of the membrane
Ca2+ do not bind to troponin
questions.e: In cardiac muscle (unlike skeletal muscle), roughly half the activator Ca2+ enters from the extracellular space via L-type Ca2+ channels, triggering further Ca2+ release from the SR (calcium-induced calcium release).

questions.q: The long plateau of the cardiac muscle action potential is due to
o: movement of fewer Na+ across the membrane
decrease in the amount of Ca2+ diffusing across the membrane
questions.e: The plateau phase is maintained by sustained opening of L-type Ca2+ channels, which balances the outward K+ current and holds the membrane depolarized.

questions.q: The most common type of synapse in the nervous system is
questions.e: Chemical synapses, using neurotransmitters, are by far the most common type in the nervous system.

questions.q: The ion that triggers the release of transmitter by a neuron is
questions.e: Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated channels at the axon terminal triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a possible drug effect on synaptic function?
o: Change the type of receptor found in the postsynaptic membrane
questions.e: Drugs can affect synthesis, reuptake, inactivation, or receptor binding of a neurotransmitter, but they do not change the actual type of receptor expressed in the membrane.

questions.q: The site of the neuron where EPSPs and IPSPs are integrated is the
questions.e: The axon hillock is where all excitatory and inhibitory graded potentials are summed to determine if threshold is reached and an action potential fires.

questions.q: EPSPs occur when
o: more Ca2+ than usual leak out of a cell
more K+ than usual leak out of a cell
questions.e: Excitatory postsynaptic potentials (EPSPs) are caused by Na+ influx, which depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane toward threshold.

questions.q: IPSPs
o: are due to an increase in Na+ efflux
are due to a decrease in K+ efflux
questions.e: Inhibitory postsynaptic potentials (IPSPs) are local hyperpolarizations (usually via Cl- influx or K+ efflux), moving the membrane further from threshold.

questions.q: Summation that results from the cumulative effect of multiple synapses at multiple places on the neuron is designated
questions.e: Spatial summation refers to the combined effect of multiple simultaneous inputs at different synaptic sites on the neuron.

questions.q: Which one of these is false about electrical synapses?
o: They are faster than chemical synapses
questions.e: Electrical synapses are typically bidirectional (current can flow either way through the connexon channels), unlike chemical synapses which are unidirectional.

questions.q: The acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction are
questions.e: The skeletal neuromuscular junction uses nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end-plate.

questions.q: Inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase can block neuromuscular transmission because
o: ACh synthesis in the presynaptic membrane is inhibited
ACh is no longer secreted by the presynaptic membrane
choline uptake is blocked by the presynaptic membrane
ACh is not degraded leading to a prolonged depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane
ACh is blocked from attaching to its receptors on the postsynaptic membrane
questions.e: Without acetylcholinesterase, ACh lingers in the synaptic cleft, causing persistent depolarization of the end-plate, which inactivates voltage-gated Na+ channels and blocks further transmission.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by
o: preventing the release of Ach by the motor neuron
competing with Ach receptors on the sarcolemma
questions.e: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins required for vesicle docking/fusion at the presynaptic membrane, preventing ACh release.

questions.q: Myasthenia gravis results from
o: loss of Ach receptors in the end-plate membrane
insufficient Ach release from the presynaptic vesicles
the motor neuron action potential being too small to shock the muscle membrane
excessive acetylcholinesterase that destroys the neurotransmitter
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies destroy/block nicotinic ACh receptors on the postsynaptic (end-plate) membrane, weakening neuromuscular transmission.

questions.q: The Ach receptors at the neuroeffector junction are
questions.e: At autonomic neuroeffector junctions (e.g. postganglionic parasympathetic endings on organs), the ACh receptors are muscarinic.

questions.q: Which one of these is not cholinergic?
o: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervating the sweat glands
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervating the heart
questions.e: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers are typically adrenergic (release noradrenaline), including those to the heart. The exception is sweat glands, which uniquely receive cholinergic postganglionic sympathetic fibers.

questions.q: Preganglionic neurons of the sympathetic nervous system synapse in the
questions.e: Sympathetic preganglionic fibers can synapse in the paravertebral (sympathetic chain) ganglia, the prevertebral ganglia, or directly innervate the adrenal medulla (a modified sympathetic ganglion).

questions.q: The receptors on sweat glands are
questions.e: Although innervated by sympathetic fibers, sweat glands (most of them) respond to ACh acting on muscarinic receptors.

questions.q: Increased sympathetic activity will result in all but one of the following.
questions.e: Sympathetic activation causes pupil dilation, ejaculation, increased heart rate, and sweating, but tear secretion is driven by parasympathetic (not sympathetic) stimulation.

questions.q: Which one of these organs has only sympathetic innervation?
questions.e: Sweat glands receive only sympathetic innervation (uniquely via cholinergic fibers); the other organs listed receive dual (sympathetic + parasympathetic) innervation.

questions.q: Which of these is not true about the parasympathetic system?
o: They have relatively long preganglionic fibers
It also called the craniosacral division of the ANS
It causes constriction of the pupils
questions.e: Sweat glands are innervated by the sympathetic (not parasympathetic) division — via cholinergic sympathetic fibers, an exception in the sympathetic system.

questions.q: Parasympathetic stimulation increases
questions.e: Parasympathetic ('rest and digest') stimulation increases gastrointestinal motility and secretion, while decreasing heart rate and contractility.

questions.q: Muscarinic receptors are blocked by
questions.e: Atropine is the classic competitive antagonist at muscarinic ACh receptors.

questions.q: The parasympathetic system is especially active during
questions.e: The parasympathetic ('rest and digest') system predominates during quiet, non-stressful activities such as digestion.

questions.q: A boy accidentally ate mushroom containing muscarine. What symptoms would you expect to observe?
questions.e: Muscarine over-stimulates muscarinic receptors, producing classic parasympathomimetic effects: diarrhea, salivation, bradycardia (low heart rate), and sweating — all of the above.

questions.q: Which of these receive only parasympathetic innervation?
questions.e: The lacrimal glands' secretory activity is under parasympathetic control only; the other structures listed receive dual sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation.

questions.q: The equilibrium potential of an ion can be calculated using the
questions.e: The Nernst equation calculates the equilibrium potential for a single ion based on its concentration gradient.

questions.e: Although innervated by sympathetic fibers, sweat glands (most of them) respond to ACh acting on muscarinic receptors.

o: Ca2+ do not bind to troponin
About half the Ca2+ required for contraction comes from outside the cell
Ca2+ plays an important role in repolarization of the membrane
Ca2+ are not released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
Ca2+ play no role in the process of contraction
questions.e: In cardiac muscle (unlike skeletal muscle), roughly half the activator Ca2+ enters from the extracellular space via L-type Ca2+ channels, triggering further Ca2+ release from the SR (calcium-induced calcium release).

questions.e: The correct order is: latent period, depolarization, repolarization, and finally after-hyperpolarization.

questions.q: When thyroxin binds to its receptor to form a hormone-receptor complex,
questions.e: Thyroxine binds an intracellular/nuclear receptor; the hormone-receptor complex acts directly on DNA to initiate gene transcription.

questions.q: A researcher compares HbA, HbA2, and HbF. Which correctly identifies the form present in the highest proportion in a healthy adult?
o: All three are present in exactly equal proportions
questions.e: HbA (α2β2) makes up about 96-98% of adult hemoglobin, making it by far the dominant form; HbA2 is a minor adult form (2-3%), and HbF is the dominant fetal form, present only in small amounts after infancy.

questions.e: Muscarine over-stimulates muscarinic receptors, producing classic parasympathomimetic effects: diarrhea, salivation, bradycardia (low heart rate), and sweating — all of the above.

questions.q: An elderly patient's red blood cells are found to be more fragile than normal and are being cleared prematurely by the spleen. What is the most direct underlying cause of this fragility as RBCs age toward the end of their 120-day lifespan?
o: Conversion of Hb A to Hb F
Gradual loss of hemoglobin from the cell
Progressive loss of ATP-generating metabolic capacity needed to maintain the cell wall
questions.e: As RBCs age, their metabolic processes (which generate the ATP needed to maintain the integrity of the cell membrane) weaken, making the cells progressively more fragile until they lyse when passing through small vascular spaces, especially in the spleen.

questions.q: The cross-bridge cycle continues as long as:
o: Troponin is in its resting conformation
Tropomyosin is blocking actin binding sites
questions.e: Cross-bridge cycling continues as long as sarcoplasmic Ca2+ remains elevated. When Ca2+ is pumped back into the SR, troponin-tropomyosin re-blocks actin, and contraction ceases.

questions.e: Troponin binds tropomyosin and, at rest (low Ca2+), holds it over the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Black widow spider venom impairs neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Disrupting synaptic vesicles and depleting nerve terminals of ACh
questions.e: Black widow spider venom disrupts synaptic vesicles and depletes the nerve terminal of ACh.

o: They generally do not integrate signals
They always require Ca2+ influx to function
They rely entirely on neurotransmitter diffusion
