questions.q: Which of these is not true about the neuronal action potential?
questions.e: An action potential is not 'always depolarizing' — it involves a depolarization phase followed by repolarization (and often after-hyperpolarization). Also, action potentials do not summate (feature b in the list is the false one; note option d 'It summates' is also false, but the classically tested false statement here is 'always depolarizing').
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: What are the two general types of cardiac action potential?
questions.e: Cardiac tissue produces two broad AP families: non-pacemaker ("fast response") potentials in working myocardium and pacemaker ("slow response") potentials in conduction tissue.

questions.q: Active transport requires which two things that facilitated diffusion does not?
questions.e: Unlike facilitated diffusion, active transport requires both a carrier protein and metabolic energy, since it moves substances against their gradient.

questions.q: Myosin binding sites on the actin filament are exposed after
questions.e: Ca2+ binding to troponin C causes a conformational change that shifts tropomyosin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin.

questions.q: Sensory "adaptation" refers to:
o: A conversion of receptor potentials into resting potentials
An increase in receptor sensitivity over time under constant stimulation
A decrease in responsiveness of receptors to a uniformly maintained stimulus of constant intensity
A permanent loss of receptor function
questions.e: Adaptation is a decrease in the responsiveness of receptors to a uniformly maintained stimulus of constant intensity, seen as declining AP frequency and a subjectively weaker stimulus over time.

questions.q: The three principal components of the plasma membrane are:
questions.e: The plasma membrane's principal components are lipids, proteins, and carbohydrates, in ratios that vary with the membrane's location and role.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a possible drug effect on synaptic function?
o: Change the type of receptor found in the postsynaptic membrane
questions.e: Drugs can affect synthesis, reuptake, inactivation, or receptor binding of a neurotransmitter, but they do not change the actual type of receptor expressed in the membrane.

questions.q: How does the duration of the cardiac muscle twitch compare with the duration of the action potential?
o: There is no relationship between the two
The twitch is almost the same duration as the AP
The twitch is much shorter than the AP
The twitch is many times longer than the AP
questions.e: The cardiac muscle twitch lasts almost as long as the action potential itself, largely because of the prolonged plateau phase.

questions.q: The two main classes of adrenergic receptors (adrenoceptors) are:
questions.e: Adrenoceptors are divided into alpha-adrenergic and beta-adrenergic receptors, each with subtypes.

questions.q: The force of a tetanic contraction is greater than that of a single twitch contraction because:
o: Tetanic stimulation recruits a larger number of individual muscle fibers than a twitch does
Twitch contractions only involve fast-twitch (Type II) fibers, which are inherently weaker
Successive stimuli arrive before the muscle can fully relax, so individual contractions summate while Ca²⁺ stays elevated, allowing continuous cross-bridge cycling
Tetany results from one large stimulus, whereas a twitch results from repeated small stimuli
questions.e: In a single twitch, the muscle has time to relax fully between the stimulus and the next possible contraction. In tetanus, stimuli arrive in rapid succession — faster than the relaxation time — so cytosolic Ca²⁺ remains persistently elevated and successive twitches mechanically summate, producing a smooth, sustained contraction with much greater force than any single twitch. (This was an open-ended question in the original paper; it has been converted into a single-best-answer item here.)

questions.q: The main function of nociceptors is to sense:
questions.e: Nociceptors are free nerve endings specialized to detect noxious (potentially damaging) stimuli — mechanical, thermal, or chemical — and transmit signals that are perceived as pain.

questions.q: The plasma membrane is approximately how thick?
questions.e: The plasma membrane is a thin, pliable, elastic structure between 7.5 and 10 nm thick.

questions.q: A patient's blood sample is centrifuged and shows a hematocrit of 55%. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
questions.e: Hematocrit reflects the percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells (normal ~42-47%). A value of 55% indicates the red cell fraction is elevated relative to plasma, consistent with dehydration (reduced plasma volume) or polycythemia (increased red cell production).

questions.q: In young women, TBW is approximately what percentage of body weight?
questions.e: TBW in young women is about 45–50% of body weight — lower than in men, largely reflecting a higher proportion of adipose tissue.

questions.q: The glial cells that form the blood-brain barrier are the
questions.e: Astrocyte end-feet surround brain capillaries and induce/maintain the tight junctions of the blood-brain barrier.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: The Ach receptors at the neuroeffector junction are
questions.e: At autonomic neuroeffector junctions (e.g. postganglionic parasympathetic endings on organs), the ACh receptors are muscarinic.

questions.q: Cardiac tension developed by the myocyte is generally proportional to:
questions.e: The tension developed by cardiac cells is proportional to intracellular Ca²⁺ concentration — more Ca²⁺ bound to troponin C means more active cross-bridges.

questions.q: The ability of smooth muscle to function over a wide range of length is called
questions.e: Plasticity allows smooth muscle to maintain tension despite changes in length (stress-relaxation response), letting it function well over a wide range of lengths (e.g. a filling bladder).

questions.q: Hemicholinium impairs neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Blocking the Na+-choline transporter, depleting choline for ACh synthesis
Degrading ACh in the synaptic cleft
questions.e: Hemicholiniums block the Na+-choline transporter, and prolonged use depletes choline needed for ACh synthesis.

questions.q: Regular (continuous) conduction is best described as:
o: Conduction that occurs only in glial cells
A hopping conduction restricted to myelinated fibers
A sequential, wave-like spread of the action potential occurring in unmyelinated axons
Conduction that requires no ion channels
questions.e: Regular/continuous conduction is the sequential spread of the action potential as a wave, characteristic of unmyelinated axons.

questions.q: A patient develops a deep vein thrombosis after a long-haul flight involving prolonged immobility. Which combination of factors most directly explains this increased clotting risk?
o: Increased blood pH and decreased platelet count
Sluggish venous blood flow during prolonged immobility, favoring thrombus formation
Increased erythropoietin secretion during the flight
questions.e: Thrombus formation is particularly favored by sluggish blood flow, which is especially relevant in veins during conditions like prolonged immobility (long flights, post-operative bed rest) — stagnant flow allows activated clotting factors to accumulate locally rather than being washed away.

questions.q: "Transduction" specifically refers to:
o: Coding stimulus intensity as AP frequency
Conversion of stimulus energy into a receptor/generator potential
Sending signals down the axon to the synapse
questions.e: Transduction is the conversion of stimulus energy into a membrane potential — a receptor potential (RP) or generator potential (GP) — that can go on to fire an action potential.

questions.q: Which of these statements about smooth muscle fibers is false?
questions.e: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; it uses calmodulin to regulate contraction via myosin light chain kinase.

questions.q: Which ionic profile best characterizes intracellular fluid (ICF)?
o: High K⁺ and Mg²⁺; low Na⁺ and Cl⁻
High Ca²⁺, with all other ions absent
High Na⁺ and Cl⁻; low K⁺ and Mg²⁺
Equal concentrations of Na⁺ and K⁺
questions.e: ICF is high in potassium, magnesium, phosphate, organic anions, and proteins, and low in sodium, bicarbonate, and chloride.

questions.q: Diffusion is best defined as:
o: Random thermal motion of molecules resulting in net flux toward lower concentration
Active pumping of molecules against a gradient
questions.e: Diffusion is the random thermal motion of molecules that results in a net flux toward regions of lower concentration, moving the system toward equilibrium.

questions.q: The long plateau of the cardiac muscle action potential is due to
o: movement of fewer Na+ across the membrane
decrease in the amount of Ca2+ diffusing across the membrane
questions.e: The plateau phase is maintained by sustained opening of L-type Ca2+ channels, which balances the outward K+ current and holds the membrane depolarized.

questions.q: In the absence of troponin, what protein does free Ca2+ bind to initiate the smooth muscle contraction cascade?
questions.e: Free Ca2+ binds to calmodulin (CM) in a 4:1 ratio, substituting functionally for the troponin-based mechanism of striated muscle.

questions.q: Which one of these is false about electrical synapses?
o: They are faster than chemical synapses
questions.e: Electrical synapses are typically bidirectional (current can flow either way through the connexon channels), unlike chemical synapses which are unidirectional.

questions.q: At what point in the ventricular action potential is the membrane most permeable to Ca²⁺?
questions.e: The plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is sustained by inward Ca²⁺ current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels, which balances outward K⁺ current — this is when Ca²⁺ permeability is at its highest, and it's also what triggers Ca²⁺-induced Ca²⁺ release for contraction.

questions.q: IP3 and DAG are both derived from the hydrolysis of which membrane lipid, catalyzed by phospholipase C?
questions.e: IP3 and DAG are synthesized from phosphatidylinositol-4,5-bisphosphate (PIP2), which PLC hydrolyzes after GPCR-mediated activation.

questions.q: Multiunit smooth muscle is characterized by which innervation pattern?
questions.e: Multiunit smooth muscle has high innervation density, consistent with its need for fine, individualized control.

questions.q: Unassisted ATP stores in muscle can sustain contraction for approximately:
questions.e: ATP stores alone can sustain contraction for only about 3 seconds. Other energy systems rapidly replenish ATP to continue contraction beyond this.

questions.q: The rapid rise and fall in force produced by a muscle fiber after a single action potential is
questions.e: A single action potential produces a single twitch — a brief rise and fall in tension.

questions.q: The main component of the lipid bilayer is:
questions.e: Phospholipids are the main components of the lipid bilayer, with hydrophilic phosphate heads and hydrophobic fatty-acid tails.

questions.q: Regarding excitation–contraction coupling, which of the following is correct?
o: The muscle action potential propagates along the sarcolemma and down the T-tubules
Relaxation occurs when Ca²⁺ is actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum via SERCA
In the resting state, tropomyosin (not troponin itself) sterically blocks the myosin-binding site on actin
The Ca²⁺ released by the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds to tropomyosin
questions.e: Excitation–contraction coupling begins with the action potential spreading along the sarcolemma and into the T-tubules, which triggers Ca²⁺ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Note: Ca²⁺ actually binds troponin (not tropomyosin) which then shifts tropomyosin off the actin binding site — so the classic textbook statement in option B is a common trap. Option A is the accurate first step of the process.

questions.q: In cardiac muscle, a T-tubule associates with a single terminal cisterna of sarcoplasmic reticulum to form a structure called a:
questions.e: This single T-tubule/single-cisterna pairing is called a diad, in contrast with the triads (one T-tubule, two cisternae) of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Which of these is classified as a neuroexciter (produces EPSPs)?
questions.e: Glutamate is a neuroexciter, along with ACh (in skeletal muscle), NE, E, dopamine, and aspartate.

questions.q: Which regulatory protein found in skeletal muscle thin filaments is absent in smooth muscle?
questions.e: No troponin is present in smooth muscle cells — this is why calcium regulation instead proceeds via calmodulin and myosin light-chain kinase.

questions.q: Tubocurarine is an example of a:
questions.e: Tubocurarine is a non-depolarizing blocker — a competitive ACh receptor antagonist at nicotinic receptors.

questions.q: Who coined the term "homeostasis," and from what language are its roots derived?
questions.e: Walter Cannon coined the term homeostasis in 1932, from the Greek words homeo (same, similar) and stasis (standing, stillness).

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about transmembrane proteins?
o: They can be removed by alkaline solutions
They are embedded in the lipid bilayer
They have both hydrophobic and hydrophilic ends
questions.e: Integral/transmembrane proteins span the bilayer and need detergents to be removed. Alkaline (or high salt) solutions only strip loosely-associated peripheral proteins.

questions.q: The myogenic response of visceral/unitary smooth muscle refers to its tendency to:
questions.e: Unitary smooth muscle contracts when stretched — a myogenic response — independent of external nervous input.

questions.q: Which of the following acts as an ATPase during the contraction of skeletal muscle?
questions.e: The myosin head has ATPase activity — it hydrolyzes ATP to power the cross-bridge cycle.

questions.q: Feedforward control is best described as:
o: A response in anticipation of a change in a controlled variable, suppressing the disturbance before it affects the system
A form of negative feedback exclusively
A delayed correction after an error has already occurred
questions.e: Feedforward control anticipates a change in a controlled variable, suppressing the disturbance before it can affect the system's essential variables.

questions.q: The function of the T-tubules in skeletal muscle is to
o: transmit APs deep into the muscle cell
release Ca2+ into the cell from the ECF
questions.e: T-tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that rapidly conduct the action potential from the cell surface deep into the interior of the muscle fiber, near the SR.

questions.q: An action potential cannot cross the synaptic cleft between neurons directly because:
o: The cleft is filled with myelin
The postsynaptic membrane has no ion channels
Na+ channels are absent from the presynaptic membrane
Transmission there is chemical, not electrical, and the cleft interrupts electrical continuity
questions.e: Because transmission at a chemical synapse is mediated by neurotransmitter diffusion rather than direct current flow, an action potential cannot 'jump' across the cleft.

questions.q: Why is Ca²⁺ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum alone insufficient to fully activate contraction in cardiac muscle?
o: Because troponin C is absent in cardiac muscle
Because the cardiac SR is relatively sparse compared with skeletal muscle
Because Ca²⁺ is toxic to cardiac cells
Because cardiac muscle has no T-tubules
questions.e: Cardiac SR is relatively sparse (less developed), so SR-released Ca²⁺ must be augmented by Ca²⁺ entering through channels in the general sarcolemma, triggered by the AP.

questions.q: The site of the neuron where EPSPs and IPSPs are integrated is the
questions.e: The axon hillock is where all excitatory and inhibitory graded potentials are summed to determine if threshold is reached and an action potential fires.

questions.q: Which one of these does not act by a cytoplasmic receptor?
questions.e: Acetylcholine is hydrophilic and binds membrane-bound receptors (nicotinic/muscarinic); steroid hormones and NO act via intracellular/cytoplasmic receptors.

questions.q: In the heart
o: sympathetic stimulation increases its force of contraction
sympathetic stimulation decreases time available for ventricular filling
questions.e: All are true: vagal stimulation slows the heart, sympathetic stimulation shortens diastole (reducing filling time) and increases contractile force (positive inotropy).

questions.q: Neurones in the CNS are myelinated by
questions.e: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons (one oligodendrocyte can myelinate multiple axons); Schwann cells perform this role in the PNS.
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: Phasic receptors, such as the Pacinian corpuscle, are characterized by:
o: Quick adaptation to stimuli such as touch, odor, temperature, and pressure
questions.e: Phasic receptors adapt quickly and are typically associated with touch, odor, temperature, and pressure sensations; the Pacinian corpuscle is a classic example.

questions.q: By simple diffusion, the direction of solute movement is always:
questions.e: The direction of movement of solutes by diffusion is always from a higher to a lower concentration.

questions.q: Myasthenia gravis results from
o: insufficient Ach release from the presynaptic vesicles
excessive acetylcholinesterase that destroys the neurotransmitter
the motor neuron action potential being too small to shock the muscle membrane
loss of Ach receptors in the end-plate membrane
questions.e: Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease in which antibodies destroy/block nicotinic ACh receptors on the postsynaptic (end-plate) membrane, weakening neuromuscular transmission.

questions.q: Most of the choline released from ACh breakdown at the NMJ is:
o: Returned to the presynaptic terminal via a Na+-choline cotransporter for ACh resynthesis
questions.e: Choline is returned to the presynaptic terminal by a Na+-choline cotransporter and combined with acetyl-CoA to resynthesize ACh.

questions.q: The FIRST step in cross-bridge cycling is:
questions.e: ATP hydrolysis is the first step: ATP binds to the myosin cross-bridge and is hydrolyzed to ADP + Pi. This energizes the myosin head and increases its affinity for actin.

questions.q: How is homeostasis best defined?
o: A one-time adjustment made at birth
The maintenance of a constant, relatively stable internal environment despite a changing external environment
The process by which cells divide and differentiate
The complete elimination of all internal fluctuations
questions.e: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant, relatively stable internal environment in the face of a changing external environment.

questions.q: Tetanic muscle contractions do not occur in a normal cardiac muscle because
o: cardiac muscle contract on its own
the refractory period lasts until the muscle relaxes
the refractory period ends before the muscle reaches peak tension
questions.e: Cardiac muscle has a long absolute refractory period that lasts almost as long as the contraction itself, preventing summation and tetanus — essential for the heart's pumping cycle.

questions.q: Uptake of molecules by caveolae is termed
questions.e: Potocytosis is the specific term for molecule uptake via caveolae (flask-shaped membrane invaginations rich in caveolin).

questions.q: The resting membrane potential (RMP) of a skeletal muscle fiber is approximately:
questions.e: The RMP of skeletal muscle fibers is approximately -90 mV, which is slightly more negative than the typical -70 mV of neurons.

questions.q: Because electrical current spreads freely between cardiac cells via gap junctions, cardiac muscle functions as a:
questions.e: The electrical continuity provided by gap junctions allows cardiac muscle to behave functionally as a single unit, or syncytium.

questions.q: At approximately what membrane potential does a pacemaker cell reach threshold and trigger phase 0?
questions.e: The slow phase 4 depolarization continues until the threshold potential, roughly −40 to −50 mV, is reached.

questions.q: Which proteins make up the non-contractile intermediate filaments of smooth muscle?
questions.e: Non-contractile intermediate filaments contain the proteins desmin or vimentin, which help relay contraction and shorten the whole cell.

questions.q: Damage to the ependymal cells would most likely affect the
questions.e: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and, together with choroid plexus cells, are involved in producing/regulating cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
questions.t: Neurons, Glial Cells & the Resting/Action Potential

questions.q: The parasympathetic system is especially active during
questions.e: The parasympathetic ('rest and digest') system predominates during quiet, non-stressful activities such as digestion.

questions.q: During the power stroke, the thin filament moves toward:
questions.e: The rotation of the myosin head (power stroke) pulls the thin filament toward the CENTER of the sarcomere (toward the M-line), shortening the sarcomere.

questions.q: The most common type of synapse in the nervous system is
questions.e: Chemical synapses, using neurotransmitters, are by far the most common type in the nervous system.

questions.q: Triads are positioned near the:
questions.e: A triad (one T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum) is located at the junction between the A band and the I band in mammalian skeletal muscle — there are two triads per sarcomere, one at each A-I junction.

questions.q: The triads in skeletal muscle are situated at the
questions.e: Triads (T-tubule flanked by two terminal cisternae of the SR) are located at the junction of the A band and I band.

questions.q: Which statement about multiunit smooth muscle electrical coupling is correct?
o: Cells are connected only by tight junctions
Cells share a common continuous membrane
Cells have extensive interconnecting bridges (gap junctions)
questions.e: Multiunit smooth muscle cells have no interconnecting bridges, so excitation of one fiber does not readily spread to its neighbors.

questions.q: Summation that results from the cumulative effect of multiple synapses at multiple places on the neuron is designated
questions.e: Spatial summation refers to the combined effect of multiple simultaneous inputs at different synaptic sites on the neuron.

questions.q: When a catecholamine binds to a membrane bound receptor, the
o: hormone-receptor complex moves into the cytoplasm
second messengers appear in the cytoplasm
hormone-receptor complex moves into the nucleus
questions.e: Catecholamines act via membrane G-protein-coupled receptors, triggering intracellular second messengers (e.g. cAMP, IP3) rather than the complex itself entering the cell.

questions.q: Two of these organ systems bear the major responsibility for ensuring homeostasis: 1. Nervous system 2. Digestive system 3. Reproductive system 4. Cardiovascular system 5. Endocrine system
questions.e: The nervous system and endocrine system are the two major regulatory systems that maintain homeostasis, communicating via electrical signals and hormones respectively.

questions.q: The latent period of a muscle twitch lasts about:
questions.e: The latent period lasts approximately 2 milliseconds — the time between stimulation and the onset of force generation, corresponding to the time required for Ca2+ release from the SR.

questions.q: Which of these is not true during oxidative phosphorylation
questions.e: Pyruvic acid is produced during glycolysis and consumed (converted to Acetyl-CoA) before oxidative phosphorylation — it is not produced during this process.

questions.q: Cardiac muscle is best classified as:
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is a type of involuntary striated muscle found only in the heart — it shares the striated (banded) appearance of skeletal muscle but contracts without conscious control.

questions.q: What happens after a ligand binds an intracellular receptor?
o: Nothing further happens inside the cell
The complex is immediately degraded by lysosomes
The receptor opens an ion channel within milliseconds
The ligand-receptor complex migrates to the nucleus and binds DNA directly, affecting gene transcription
questions.e: Upon ligand binding, intracellular receptors migrate to the nucleus, where the ligand-receptor complex directly binds a region of DNA and affects gene transcription.

questions.q: Which one of these is not controlled by negative feedback mechanism?
questions.e: The pre-ovulatory LH surge is a classic example of positive feedback — rising estrogen further stimulates LH release rather than inhibiting it.

questions.q: The Frank–Starling principle states that stroke volume increases in response to:
o: An increase in end-diastolic volume filling the heart
A decrease in heart rate alone
questions.e: The Frank–Starling principle: stroke volume increases in response to an increase in the volume of blood filling the heart (the end-diastolic volume), reflecting the underlying length–tension relationship of ventricular fibres.

questions.q: The type of contraction in which the muscle fiber does not shorten is called
questions.e: Isometric contraction generates tension without a change in muscle length.

questions.q: If a man's plasma volume is 3 litres and hematocrit is 0.40, what will his total blood volume be?
questions.e: Blood volume = Plasma volume ÷ (1 − hematocrit) = 3 ÷ (1 − 0.40) = 3 ÷ 0.6 = 5 l.

questions.q: Type I muscle fibers are best characterized as:
o: Slow oxidative, fatigue-resistant, rich in myoglobin
questions.e: Type I (Slow Oxidative) fibers are loaded with mitochondria, rich in myoglobin (red), highly fatigue-resistant, have extensive blood supply, and are innervated by slow-conducting small neurons.

questions.q: Extracellular fluid (ECF) comprises what fraction of total body water?
questions.e: ECF comprises the remaining 1/3 of TBW, found outside the cells.

questions.q: Series Elastic Elements (SEE) in muscle include:
o: Muscle membranes parallel to contractile elements
questions.e: Series Elastic Elements are in series with the contractile elements and include titin and tendons. They lengthen slightly during contraction and allow a contracted muscle to stretch past L0.

questions.q: The enzyme that rapidly degrades ACh at the neuromuscular junction is:
questions.e: AChE, bound to the postjunctional membrane and other structures in the cleft, rapidly degrades ACh.

questions.q: The heart is innervated by
questions.e: The heart receives dual innervation — vagal (parasympathetic) fibers slow it down and sympathetic fibers speed it up / increase its force.

questions.q: A patient with a severe vessel injury shows an initial, immediate reduction in blood flow to the area even before any platelet plug has formed. What accounts for this earliest hemostatic response?
o: Formation of a stable fibrin clot
Local vasoconstriction, via smooth muscle contraction in the vessel wall
questions.e: The very first hemostatic response to vessel injury is local vasoconstriction — contraction of smooth muscle in the injured vessel wall — which reduces blood flow to the area even before platelet aggregation or clot formation has begun.

questions.q: What happens when Ca2+-calmodulin (CaCM) binds caldesmon?
o: Caldesmon is released from the tropomyosin/actin complex, permitting myosin binding
questions.e: Binding of CaCM to caldesmon releases caldesmon from the tropomyosin/actin complex, so myosin can now bind to the thin filament.

questions.q: Which one of these is not cholinergic?
o: Postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervating the heart
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervating the sweat glands
questions.e: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers are typically adrenergic (release noradrenaline), including those to the heart. The exception is sweat glands, which uniquely receive cholinergic postganglionic sympathetic fibers.

questions.q: Which of the following lists the components of the heart's conduction system?
o: SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibres, internodal pathways
Only the SA node and AV node
Bundle of His and coronary sinus only
questions.e: The conduction system comprises the SA node, atrial internodal pathways, the AV node, the Bundle of His, and Purkinje fibres.

questions.q: The neuroeffector junction is the termination of a postganglionic autonomic nerve upon:
o: Smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and secretory tissue
questions.e: The neuroeffector junction is where postganglionic autonomic fibres terminate on smooth/cardiac muscle and glands.

questions.q: Once generated at one site on an axon, how is an action potential conducted along the rest of the axon?
o: By direct transmission through the myelin sheath only
By local current flow between active and adjacent inactive regions
By diffusion of neurotransmitter along the axon interior
questions.e: Action potentials are conducted along the axon by local current flow: positive charges spread from the active site toward the adjacent inactive region, driving it to threshold.

questions.q: The ion that triggers the release of transmitter by a neuron is
questions.e: Ca2+ influx through voltage-gated channels at the axon terminal triggers vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a second messenger?
questions.e: RGS (Regulator of G-protein Signaling) is a protein that accelerates GTP hydrolysis on G-alpha subunits — it is a signalling regulator, not a second messenger.

questions.q: A clinician orders both a bleeding time and a clotting time on a patient with unexplained bruising. The bleeding time is prolonged but the clotting time is normal. Which category of disorder does this pattern most strongly suggest?
o: A deficiency of intrinsic pathway clotting factors (e.g., factor IX)
A deficiency isolated to Factor XII alone
Normal clotting cascade function throughout, ruling out any disorder
A platelet or vascular disorder, or extrinsic pathway deficiency, rather than an intrinsic/common pathway problem
questions.e: Bleeding time specifically reflects platelet function, vascular integrity, and the extrinsic pathway, while clotting time reflects the intrinsic and common pathways. A prolonged bleeding time with a normal clotting time points toward a platelet, vascular, or extrinsic pathway problem rather than an intrinsic pathway factor deficiency.

questions.q: Smooth muscle relaxation is associated with which change in intracellular calcium?
o: A shift of Ca2+ into the nucleus
A sustained rise in intracellular Ca2+
questions.e: Smooth muscle relaxation is associated with low intracellular Ca2+ concentrations, achieved by extrusion and reuptake mechanisms.

questions.q: A smooth, sustained contraction without any evidence of relaxation resulting from very rapid stimulation of the muscle is called
questions.e: Complete tetanus occurs when stimulation is fast enough that individual twitches fuse completely into one smooth, sustained contraction.

questions.q: T-tubules are contiguous with which membrane system?
questions.e: T-tubules (transverse tubules) are tube-like invaginations of the sarcolemma (the muscle cell membrane) that dive deep into the fiber, allowing the action potential to reach the interior of the cell rapidly and uniformly.

questions.q: A single motor neuron and all the muscle fibers it innervates is called
questions.e: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron plus all the muscle fibers it innervates.

questions.q: The width of the junctional cleft at neuroeffector junctions:
o: Is always wider than at the NMJ
Is fixed at 20 nm in every organ
Varies widely, roughly 10 to 2000 nm, between organs
Is identical to the electrical synapse gap junction width
questions.e: The junctional cleft width at neuroeffector junctions varies considerably (10–2000 nm) between organs.

questions.q: Increased sympathetic activity will result in all but one of the following.
questions.e: Sympathetic activation causes pupil dilation, ejaculation, increased heart rate, and sweating, but tear secretion is driven by parasympathetic (not sympathetic) stimulation.

questions.q: Which one of these cannot be measured directly using a marker?
questions.e: There is no marker that distributes only in the interstitial space; it is calculated indirectly as ECF volume minus plasma volume.

questions.q: Which one of these organs has only sympathetic innervation?
questions.e: Sweat glands receive only sympathetic innervation (uniquely via cholinergic fibers); the other organs listed receive dual (sympathetic + parasympathetic) innervation.

questions.q: Before receiving a signal, where is the G protein located relative to its receptor?
o: Free-floating on the cytoplasmic side of the membrane, not normally bound to the receptor
questions.e: The G protein is not normally bound to the receptor but is free-floating in the cell membrane on the cytoplasmic side.

questions.q: What binds the alpha subunit of an inactive (resting) G protein?
questions.e: The inactive form of the G protein has GDP bound to the alpha subunit, along with beta and gamma subunits.

questions.q: In skeletal muscle at rest, the myosin binding sites on actin filaments are blocked by
questions.e: Tropomyosin physically covers the myosin-binding sites on actin at rest; troponin regulates the position of tropomyosin.

questions.q: The axon emerges from the soma at a specialized region called the:
questions.e: The axon is a long, uniform-diameter extension from the soma that emerges at the axon hillock and conducts impulses away from the cell body.

questions.q: Which of the following is a possible outcome of the "response" stage of signal transduction?
o: Immediate cell death in every case
Complete reversal of the original stimulus with no cellular change
Turning on a gene, activating an enzyme, or rearranging the cytoskeleton
questions.e: The transduction pathway triggers a response such as turning on a gene, activating an enzyme, or rearranging the cytoskeleton; there is usually an amplification of the signal.

questions.q: A smooth, sustained contraction with NO relaxation between stimuli is called:
questions.e: Complete (fused) tetanus occurs when stimulation is so rapid that no relaxation occurs between twitches, producing a smooth sustained contraction about 4 times greater than a single twitch.

questions.q: The adequate stimulus of nociceptors is
questions.e: Nociceptors respond to noxious/tissue-damaging stimuli, generating the sensation of pain — the best-fit answer among the options given.

questions.q: The neuromuscular (myoneural) junction is the synapse between:
o: A gland cell and a neuron
A sensory neuron and a receptor cell
A motor neuron terminal and the motor end plate of a muscle fibre
questions.e: The NMJ is the synapse of a motor neuron terminal with the motor end plate of a muscle fibre.

questions.q: Muscarinic receptors are blocked by
questions.e: Atropine is the classic competitive antagonist at muscarinic ACh receptors.

questions.q: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic clotting pathways ultimately converge on activation of which single factor, marking the start of the common pathway?
questions.e: Both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways converge on the activation of Factor X to Xa, which marks the beginning of the common pathway, ultimately leading to thrombin generation and fibrin formation.

questions.q: The voltage-dependent calcium channels found in the membrane of the T tubules are called
questions.e: Dihydropyridine receptors (DHPRs) are the voltage sensors/Ca2+ channels in the T-tubule membrane that mechanically couple to ryanodine receptors on the SR.

questions.q: Regarding the cell membrane, which of the following is FALSE?
o: The membrane's fluidity is increased by unsaturated fatty acid tails in the phospholipids
The hydrophilic part of the cell membrane is at the interior side of the cell membrane
About 50% of the cell membrane is made up of protein
The proteins of the cell membrane function as channels, carriers, enzymes and receptors
questions.e: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer: the hydrophilic (polar) heads face outward on BOTH surfaces (toward the extracellular fluid and toward the cytoplasm), while the hydrophobic tails point inward, forming the membrane's non-polar core. Saying the hydrophilic part is only 'at the interior side' is incorrect — that describes the hydrophobic tails, not the heads. (Note: option D was left incomplete in the original paper and has been reconstructed here as a true statement to complete the option set.)

questions.q: The most important factor in decreasing the intracellular Ca2+ concentration in skeletal muscle is
o: diffusion of Ca2+ out of the cell
active transport of Ca2+ into the synaptic cleft
active transport of Ca2+ across the sarcolemma
diffusion of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasm reticulum
active transport of Ca2+ into the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.e: The SERCA pump actively transports Ca2+ back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which is the primary mechanism lowering cytosolic Ca2+ and allowing relaxation.

questions.q: Phase 0 of the pacemaker action potential is due to an increase in conductance and inward current of which ion, through which channel type?
questions.e: Unlike non-pacemaker phase 0 (fast Na⁺-driven), pacemaker phase 0 depolarization is due to increased Ca²⁺ conductance and inward current through L-type Ca²⁺ channels.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of primary active transport?
questions.e: Primary active transport pumps include the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, and H⁺-K⁺ ATPase, which use ATP directly.

questions.q: Membrane transport is governed by which two basic processes?
questions.e: Transport across the plasma membrane is governed by two basic processes: diffusion/passive transport and active transport.

questions.q: The enzyme responsible for conversion of ATP to cAMP is
questions.e: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP to cAMP; phosphodiesterase later breaks cAMP down, terminating the signal.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effect of sympathetic activation on pacemaker rate?
o: Increases g_K+ and suppresses I_f, decreasing rate
Decreases g_K+ and enhances the pacemaker current, increasing rate
Has no measurable effect on ion conductances
questions.e: Sympathetic activation decreases g_K+, enhances I_f, and increases slow inward g_Ca2+ and g_Na+ — steepening phase 4 and increasing pacemaker rate.

questions.q: The normal pacemaker of the heart is the
questions.e: The SA node has the fastest intrinsic rate of spontaneous depolarization and normally sets the heart rate.

questions.q: The PRIMARY function of the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle is to:
questions.e: The primary function of the sarcoplasmic reticulum is to store Ca2+ and release them during excitation-contraction coupling to trigger contraction.

questions.q: Which protein binds tropomyosin/actin and blocks myosin binding in the relaxed state?
questions.e: Caldesmon binds to the tropomyosin/actin complex and blocks the binding of myosin to actin, keeping the muscle in the relaxed state until Ca2+ rises.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by
o: preventing the release of Ach by the motor neuron
competing with Ach receptors on the sarcolemma
questions.e: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins required for vesicle docking/fusion at the presynaptic membrane, preventing ACh release.

questions.q: The acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction are
questions.e: The skeletal neuromuscular junction uses nicotinic ACh receptors on the motor end-plate.

questions.q: Which receptor type responds to dissolved chemicals in taste and smell, as well as internal chemistry changes like O2, CO2, and H+ levels?
questions.e: Chemoreceptors respond to dissolved chemicals during taste and smell sensations, as well as to changes in internal body chemistry such as O2, CO2, or H+ variations.

questions.q: Botulinum toxin blocks neuromuscular transmission by:
o: Preventing vesicular docking and thus ACh release
questions.e: Botulinum toxin blocks ACh release by preventing vesicular docking at the presynaptic membrane.

questions.q: According to the length–tension relationship in cardiac muscle, an increase in preload (within limits) leads to:
o: An increase in active tension and the rate of its development
questions.e: Within limits, increasing preload (fibre length) increases both the active tension developed and the rate at which that tension develops.

questions.q: Which one of these is not true about plasma membranes?
o: It is involved in cell to cell communication
questions.e: The lipid bilayer is actually poorly permeable to ions; ions cross mainly through specific channels/transporters, not by free diffusion.

questions.q: Parallel Elastic Elements (PEE) in muscle produce tension when the muscle is:
questions.e: PEE (provided by muscle membranes, endomysium, perimysium, and epimysium) produce tension when a muscle is PASSIVELY STRETCHED past its resting length L0.

questions.q: Blood collected into a tube containing sodium citrate does not clot in the tube. What is the mechanism by which citrate prevents clotting in this collection tube?
o: Citrate binds and removes free calcium, which is essential for the clotting cascade to proceed
Citrate activates the fibrinolytic system to dissolve any clot immediately
questions.e: Citrate (like oxalate) works by chelating (binding and removing) free calcium ions. Since calcium (Factor IV) is an essential cofactor at multiple steps of the clotting cascade, its removal prevents the sample from clotting in the collection tube.

questions.q: In the plasma membrane, carbohydrates:
o: Always face inward, towards the non-polar portion of the membrane
Always face outward, towards extracellular space
Always face the lumen of the cell
Are directed to all sides in the membrane
questions.e: Membrane carbohydrates are attached to lipids (glycolipids) or proteins (glycoproteins) exclusively on the outer leaflet, forming the glycocalyx. This layer faces the extracellular space and is involved in cell recognition, adhesion, and protection — it never faces the cytoplasmic side.

questions.q: The synaptic cleft between two neurons in a chemical synapse is approximately how wide?
questions.e: The synaptic cleft between neurons is about 20 nm wide.

questions.q: The output of a neuron representing the algebraic sum of all excitatory and inhibitory potentials from its synapses is called:
questions.e: The GPSP is the sum of all excitatory and inhibitory potentials from all of a cell's synapses, forming its single output.

questions.q: Which one of these is not a characteristic of visceral smooth muscle?
o: The fibers behave as a syncytium
They do not have a stable membrane potential
questions.e: Visceral (single-unit) smooth muscle has sparse/low innervation density; cells are instead coupled by gap junctions and behave as a functional syncytium.

questions.q: A patient with a deep laceration to a large artery is brought to the emergency room with uncontrolled bleeding. Why do the body's natural hemostatic mechanisms often fail to stop bleeding from a large artery on their own, unlike a minor capillary cut?
o: Large arteries have no smooth muscle in their walls
Platelets cannot function in arterial blood under any circumstance
Large arteries lack any hemostatic mechanisms at all
The high pressure and flow in large arteries can overwhelm the local vasoconstriction and platelet plug response that is normally effective for smaller vessels
questions.e: Hemostatic mechanisms (vasoconstriction, platelet plug) are most effective for the smaller arterioles, capillaries, and venules; the high pressure and flow of larger arteries can overwhelm these natural mechanisms, which is why bleeding from a major artery typically requires external intervention.
